aborted_first_attempt.second_outage: The restarted poll was itself cut off by a second session limit on 2026-09-29 after 40 of 75 books. packet_defect_found_and_fixed.what: Account packets showed legs closed by a standing order as live positions.
packet_defect_found_and_fixed.found_by: A manager, not the desk. Sonnet growth at a reasonable price reported that its SOXL short was listed with a running -15.51% mark five sessions after its own stop fired on 2026-09-21, and declined to trade against the number.
packet_defect_found_and_fixed.detail: tracker/desk_packets.py rendered the registered book spec and marked every leg to the latest price without checking whether a stop or take-profit had already closed it. The packet separately listed the fired orders, so each affected packet contradicted itself. The scoring engine was never wrong — on a trigger it sets the position dead, zeroes its value and banks the proceeds — but the manager's view of its own account was, and that is the input to every decision.

Two things broke the premise this book was built on. First, my entry thesis was explicitly 'repricing to $103 WTI on stale sell-side estimates.' WTI closed 2026-09-28 at ~$93, not $103 - the $103-105 print is BRENT, and the ~$12 Brent-WTI dislocation is itself a Hormuz artifact. So the number I underwrote never applied to my most WTI-levered barrels. Second, and worse, energy is no longer cheap on my own mandate's test: COP at 12.4x and CVX at 12.7x forward are ABOVE-average multiples on war-inflated peak earnings, which is the textbook value trap, and the live near-term catalyst is asymmetric against me - Iran has offered to reopen the strait within seven days for sanctions relief, and a deal takes the supply shock out. That is a geopolitical binary, not a deep-value bet, and I was carrying it at 35% of the book. I cut energy 35%->19%, eliminating COP (purest E&P/WTI beta, worst leg at -4.90%, and a brand-new CEO) and keeping an integrated, Brent-weighted stub in CVX/XOM so I still own the right tail if Trump resumes bombing after the November midterms as he has told aides he will. The proceeds go where my mandate actually points: Cigna at 8.59x forward is the cheapest large-cap defensive I can find and my strategy of record has named 'managed care at 9-11x' for weeks while I owned none of it, and CVS fell 4.22% straight into a guidance RAISE ($7.30-7.50 -> $7.90-8.10 on an $87.85 stock, ~11x). I am also repositioning for the rate regime rather than against it: Warsh has called inflation 'too high for too long,' the 10-year is above 5%, and one more hike is priced. That makes the XLP short the single best-supported leg in the book (21.4x, 2.67% yield vs a 5%+ risk-free rate), so it goes 8%->11%, while PFE - a 6.1% yielder and my most rate-sensitive long, already +4.59% - gets trimmed into strength. Citi gets a point: rising rates help NIM, and 1.3x tangible book with 11%+ RoTCE and a $30B buyback is the cheapest way I own that. Net long falls 70%->64%; gross and cash are unchanged, so turnover is roughly a third of the book and costs a few basis points - cheap relative to owning a falsified premise at 35% weight.
decisions.strategy: Concentrated long in sub-market-multiple, FCF-rich cash returners, rotated out of crude-price beta now trading at 12.4-12.7x on war-inflated peak earnings and into the cheapest defensives in the market (managed care at 8.6x, pharma at 11x, a 1.3x-book bank), with a residual Brent-weighted energy stub kept for Hormuz tail risk and an enlarged short in 21x consumer-staples bond proxies against a 5%+ 10-year.

positions.thesis: The Cigna Group at $271.83, 8.59x forward earnings - the cheapest large-cap defensive in the US market and roughly half the sector multiple. My strategy of record has specified 'managed care at 9-11x' for weeks while the book owned no pure managed-care name; this fixes that gap with the cheapest one rather than the most popular. The discount is sentiment, not fundamentals: the stock is down ~10% over a year on medical-cost-trend fear, but the sector just repriced that fear - Humana, UNH and Cigna all rallied on analysts flagging SOFTER medical cost trends, and Elevance signalled Q3 tracking ahead of a reaffirmed >=$27 guide. Cigna is also the least Medicare-Advantage-exposed of the majors, so it carries less of the MLR risk the multiple is punishing, and Evernorth's PBM cash flow funds buybacks against a shrinking share count. Largest single weight because it is the highest-conviction mispricing I found; 13% rather than more because Q3 prints in October and MLR lines can gap. Wide 18% stop to survive one bad MLR quarter; 45% target is only a re-rate to ~12.5x, still below the sector.

Adding 10%->12% on weakness against improving facts, which is the whole point of a deep-value mandate. CVS raised FY26 adjusted EPS guidance to $7.90-8.10 from $7.30-7.50 - an ~8% raise - and enterprise adjusted operating income to $16.58-16.92bn, yet the stock is DOWN 4.22% on my leg and closed at $87.85, about 11x the raised number. It reclaimed its 200-day EMA on 9/25 (+4.8%) before giving it back, so the tape is starting to notice. Consensus target is $111 with ~85% buys. Aetna expanding bundled prior authorizations in oncology is a real margin-and-utilization lever, not a press release. The known bear case is a 2027 cost headwind, which is precisely why it is cheap now and why I want it before the Q3 print rather than after. Keeping the wide 20% stop because managed-care guidance risk is genuinely two-sided.

Raised 11%->12% because this is the one leg the new rate regime makes strictly better. Tangible book per share was $100.89 at 6/30/26, up 7% year over year, against a $131.31 close - about 1.30x tangible book for a bank now guiding RoTCE slightly ABOVE 11%, with a CET1 of 12.78% versus an 11.6% requirement. That excess capital is being returned hard: $10.3bn repurchased in H1 2026 alone and a new $30bn authorization to run over two years, which on a ~$250bn cap retires a large share count at a premium-free multiple. With Warsh hawkish, the 10-year above 5% and another hike priced, net interest income and reinvestment yields work in Citi's favour while my bond-proxy short works the same thesis from the other side. Trimmed-multiple risk is credit, hence the wide 20% stop.

Trimmed 14%->11%, taking profit on my best long (+4.59%) for a specific reason: at a 6.1% forward dividend yield this is the most duration-like equity I own, and with the 10-year above 5% a 6.1% yielder no longer carries a meaningful spread over risk-free. That is a compression risk I want smaller, not gone. Still a core holding, because the single biggest overhang has been removed rather than deferred - under the April 2 Section 232 order on patented pharmaceuticals, which threatened duties up to 100%, Pfizer's applicable tariff rate is ZERO until January 20, 2029 in exchange for onshoring commitments, effective since July 31. That is three years of policy certainty the ~9x multiple is not paying for, and the 2025 revenue decline of only ~1.6% on $62.6bn says the LOE cliff is being absorbed. History also supports holding through hikes: pharma performance in 2022-23 was driven by patent and pipeline facts, not the funds rate.

Enlarged 8%->11% - the best-supported leg in the book under the new regime, and my hedge. Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR closed at $82.28 on 21.4x earnings with a 2.67% dividend yield. Against a 10-year above 5%, an investor is being asked to pay 21x for low-single-digit growth to collect less than half the risk-free rate, which is the definition of a bond proxy that has not repriced. Warsh has now said inflation 'is too high and has been for too long,' the Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00% on 12-0, the dot plot carries another 25bp in 2026 and markets price hikes extending into 2027 - so the discount rate that inflated this multiple keeps rising. Staples also face the margin side of the same oil-driven inflation that is lifting my energy stub, giving the pair an internal hedge. Holding it against a 75% long book cuts net exposure to 64% and cushions drawdown. The 10% stop is deliberately wide for a low-beta ETF - the desk just saw four short legs stopped out by a single 1.55% SPY rally, and I will not be shaken out of a hedge by beta.

Cut 15%->11%: still my primary energy holding but no longer a core bet, because at 12.68x forward it is an above-average multiple on war-inflated earnings. I keep Chevron over ConocoPhillips because it is integrated - downstream margins widen as crude falls, which is exactly the cushion I want if Iran and Washington settle and the Hormuz premium drains out of the tape. It is also the better cash compounder at this size: a 3.45% yield covered by FCF, a plan to double its operated rig count in Venezuela and LNG optionality in Argentina and the Mediterranean, all of which are volume growth that does not require $100 oil. Consensus is $223.92 across 25 analysts with HSBC at $250. The CEO's warning that depleted crude buffers point to higher prices is the right-tail case, and it is live: Trump rejected Tehran's conditional reopening offer and has told aides he expects to resume bombing after the November midterms.

Raised 7%->8%, the only energy leg I am adding to, specifically to exploit the dislocation my old thesis misread. Brent settled at $105.48 on 2026-09-28 while WTI was $93.12 - a ~$12 spread opened by the Hormuz closure. Exxon's growth barrels are Guyana and Permian-plus-international, weighting its realizations toward the Brent side of that spread, so it captures the actual $105 print rather than the $93 one that my WTI-levered legs are stuck with. It is also the steadiest leg through a resolution scenario: the largest integrated downstream and chemicals base in the group absorbs crude weakness, and the balance sheet carries the lowest leverage among the majors. Held at only 8% because, like all energy here, it is priced on cyclically elevated earnings; this is a relative-value tilt inside a shrunken sleeve, not an increase in oil risk.

Unchanged at 8% - the thesis has neither improved nor broken, so I am not paying spread to move it. Bristol Myers guides 2026 non-GAAP EPS of $6.05-6.35, putting it near 11x forward, with a 4.1% dividend yield. Critically, at 4.1% it is far less exposed to the yield-compression risk that made me trim Pfizer: the payout is roughly two-thirds covered by the growth portfolio rather than by the legacy LOE assets, so it is a cheap earnings stream rather than a stretched coupon. Like Pfizer it sits behind the Section 232 drug-pricing settlements that gave major drugmakers multi-year tariff reprieves, removing the policy tail that was suppressing the multiple. Flat +0.44% on the leg - it has done nothing, which at 11x is fine.

decisions.reason: I restructured this book eight trading days ago (2026-09-16) on an explicit macro call: a ~5% 10-year Treasury has repriced every low-yield bond-proxy defensive, while a $100+ oil shock pays the energy dividend growers directly. Every leg of that call has strengthened since, so the right action is to let it work rather than pay basis points to re-express a view I already hold. Rates: the 10-year closed 2026-09-28 at ~5.21-5.25%, a 20-year high and still climbing; the Fed hiked 25bp to 3.75-4% on 9/16 in a 12-0 vote with a dot plot signalling one more hike in 2026, against core PCE above 3% every month this year. Oil: Brent settled ~$105.28 on 9/28 after trading as high as $108.83, diesel set a record $6.06/gal on 9/11, and Iran's president publicly refused to back down on 9/23 (oil +4%). This is a military supply shock with no visible diplomatic off-ramp; the 9/28 intraday fade was a Saudi East-West pipeline repair, not a peace deal. Leg-level research confirmed rather than contradicted the book. SCHD (34% core) is +20% YTD versus SPY +13% at a 3.2% forward yield - its 10-year dividend-growth screen is precisely the right filter for this regime. CVX (15%) is +36.9% in 2026, the second-best Dow component, with HSBC raising its target to $250 from $218 on 9/25, RBC reiterating Buy, and the new Venezuela JV set to roughly double production to ~600kbpd; my -2.44% mark is entry timing, having bought eight days after a $217 local high, not thesis damage. MDT (7%) raised FY27 guidance on 9/1 to 7.25-7.75% organic growth on Q1 revenue up 13.7% that beat by $206M, and UBS lifted its target to $110 against an $89.50 mark - the softness is most plausibly arbitrage pressure into the MiniMed exchange-offer expiry on 10/9, a mechanical overhang that clears, so selling now would be selling the discount. EPD (5%) is my worst mark at -3.78% but raised its distribution 2.8% in mid-September on a 28-year growth streak, record Q2 DCF of $2.3B at 1.9x coverage, and guidance for double-digit EBITDA and DCF growth in 2027; a ~7% current yield is short-duration cash flow, exactly what you want to own when the discount rate is 5.25%. ABBV and JNJ are both marking positive and doing their defensive job. The single weakest leg is USB, down from a $65.42 August high to $58.78 with the KBW regional index off 1.5% on hike day, but a 3.75-4% funds rate against a 5.25% ten-year is a steep, NIM-positive curve for one of the best deposit franchises in the country, and I will not pay spread to exit a 5% position on sector beta. Nothing I found broke a thesis. All eight leg P&Ls sit inside +/-4% against stops set at 10-12%, which is noise over eight sessions, and the book's +2.84% NAV trails SPY's +3.26% only marginally while carrying a much shallower -3.44% max drawdown. My risk controls are already correct and live: stops on all eight legs, take-profits on the five names most exposed to an oil reversal or a further rate shock, and 12% cash earning 4% as dry powder if the Iran premium unwinds or the 10-year breaks 5.5%. Churning a confirmed thesis on eight days of noise is how a good book gets traded into a mediocre one.

The refining trade that was 52% of my gross has broken, and a momentum book is obliged to act on that rather than average into it. Three things changed since the 2026-09-21 fill. First, a catalyst: on 2026-09-23 Washington signaled a possible diesel export ban in response to surging domestic pump prices, and VLO fell 4.1% on the day with MPC and PSX following. That is a direct policy cap on the exact variable the thesis was long - the crack spread - and it is the kind of regime break that momentum systems must respect instead of rationalize. Second, the entry criterion has failed on its own terms: my strategy of record bought refiners because they were the only group printing fresh 52-week highs with accelerating 1-week returns, and as of the 2026-09-28 close six of six refining legs are red (CLMT -9.5%, CVI -4.5%, MPC -3.2%, PSX -3.1%, DINO -2.8%, VLO -0.9%) and the group is absent from every fresh-high list I can find for the week of 22-29 September. The reason to own them has been withdrawn by the tape. Third, the setup is a late-stage extreme, not an early trend: MPC, VLO and DINO are each up over 80% in 2026 against an 11% S&P, the Gulf Coast 3-2-1 crack is $39/bbl against $24 a year earlier, and the run was already being flagged in August as nearly unprecedented with normalization risk from Russian refinery restarts and Chinese product exports. Buying the ninth month of a parabolic commodity-margin move after its policy catalyst turns hostile is the opposite of what this mandate is for. Where the momentum actually is now is unambiguous and I am following it. Health Care was 7 of the 8 S&P 500 names at 52-week highs on 2026-09-28 and 3 of 6 large caps, driven by a real re-rating - XBI +55% since June 1, a wave of $1B+ pharma deals against $300B of looming loss-of-exclusivity, and AI-driven drug discovery. Alongside it sits AI-levered tech: META +36% on the month and its best month since 2013 on the Muse assistant launch, AMD +31.1% at a fresh high, OKTA +28% with Oktane AI-agent target raises. I am keeping the four legs that are still working or still at highs - AMD, AAPL, CRWD and cash discipline - and recycling the refining, tanker and stale-hardware sleeve (VLO, MPC, DINO, PSX, CVI, CLMT, FRO, DELL) into those two live trends. Turnover is roughly 60% of the book, which costs about 2bps a side and is trivially worth paying to stop financing a thesis the tape has already voted against. I am sizing META largest at 16% because it is the strongest large-cap trend in the market, but a 36% month is itself a risk, so it carries a 15% stop rather than the wider band I give the genuinely high-beta names. Cash stays at 10% - slightly tighter than the 14% I carried, because the opportunity set here is better than it was a week ago.
decisions.strategy: Concentrated long-only US price momentum re-ranked out of the broken refining/crack complex and into the two groups actually printing fresh 52-week highs with accelerating 1-month returns - AI-levered mega/large-cap tech and the biotech/life-sciences tools cohort - with trend-break stops sized to each leg's realized volatility.

This is momentum with an identifiable earnings-relevant catalyst rather than multiple expansion alone - Muse feeds the ad machine that already funds the company. Largest leg because a momentum mandate should own the strongest trend, but explicitly stopped tighter at 15% than my high-beta names: a stock that has just run 36% in a month has real air beneath it, and I want to be taken out on a trend break rather than ride a round trip.

Held and upsized from 5% to 13%. AMD is at a fresh 52-week high with a +31.1% one-month gain against +1.0% for the S&P, the best large-cap momentum reading outside META. My leg is only -1.24% because I bought it near the high on 21 September - the position is flat while the stock is at a high, which is exactly the signature of a name that consolidated and broke out rather than one that failed. It was undersized relative to the strength of its signal when the book's risk was being spent on refiners; with that capital freed, this gets a real weight. Moderate 12% stop for a moderate-volatility name.

Its function in the book is to be the low-volatility ballast in a sleeve that otherwise holds META, AMD and OKTA; the 10% stop is tight because a $5T company breaking 10% is a market event, not noise.

decisions.reason: New facts, not drift, drove this. My mandate is net-cash compounders and I had explicitly rebalanced away from second-derivative AI-capex exposure - but research this week shows two of my five holdings have become the capex problem rather than an escape from it. Meta's free cash flow fell 91% year over year to $784M as quarterly capex hit $30.1B (~98% of operating cash flow), buybacks are halted so every vesting grant now dilutes me, and management is weighing a multi-billion equity raise; that is a cash-consuming, dilution-issuing capital story, the opposite of what this book is for, so it goes to zero - and I am selling it at +6.4% into strength rather than after the raise is announced. Alphabet turned free cash flow negative in Q2 2026 for the first time ever with long-term debt doubling to $98B against $175-185B of 2026 capex; it is still a great asset (Cloud +82%, the ad-exchange antitrust win, Gemini distribution), but at 25.5x FORWARD earnings versus 17x trailing the depreciation wave is already visible in estimates, so it drops from my top weight of 24% to a normal 14%. The proceeds go where the cash actually is: NVDA at 19x forward with $120B of net income (+65%) and a record $150B buyback increase taking capacity to $235B is, ironically, now the most shareholder-cash-generative name I own, and TSM at 19.9x forward is compounding operating income +65% on pricing power. V rises to top weight because it is the purest expression of the mandate in this regime - asset-light, ~65% operating margins, no AI capex, and volume linked to nominal spend, which is exactly what rises when the Fed is hiking into sticky inflation. The macro is the second driver: the Fed hiked to 3.75-4.00%, the 10-year is above 5.2% and the 30-year is at 2004 highs. Rather than hide in cash, which loses in real terms when inflation is the problem, I bought the volatility itself - CME's rates complex is over half its volume, August ADV was its second-highest ever with Treasury ADV +15%, and it earns interest on member margin deposits, so it gets paid by the same bond rout that would compress my growth multiples. Turnover is ~45% of the book, costing roughly 2bps all-in, which is far too cheap to justify holding a position I no longer believe in.
decisions.strategy: Concentrated long book of five wide-moat, high-ROIC franchises that FUND their own growth out of operating cash flow - V, NVDA, TSM, GOOGL, CME - exiting Meta and halving Alphabet after both turned into negative-free-cash-flow AI-capex borrowers, and adding CME as a wide-moat compounder whose earnings rise with the rate volatility that is the main threat to the rest of the book, against 17% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Top weight because Visa is the one holding whose economics IMPROVE in the current regime. It is a toll booth on nominal consumer spending, so an inflation the Fed is still hiking against flows straight into payment volume, and with essentially no capital intensity it has no AI-capex hole to fund - it converts nearly all operating profit to cash at ~65% operating margins and keeps buying back stock while Meta and Alphabet cannot. The structural bear case was always disintermediation by stablecoins; this quarter inverted it - Visa now runs 160+ stablecoin-linked card programs with volume up ~200% y/y, stablecoin settlement past a $20B annualized run rate (15x a year ago), and it operates a validator node on Circle's Arc L1, so the supposed disruptor is becoming an additional rail it monetizes. At 25.4x forward for a duopoly with this durability I am happy to size up, and the 14% stop is tight because this is a low-beta name where a 14% drawdown would signal something genuinely broken rather than noise.

Raised from 15% because the buyback authorization resolved my main mandate objection. My book is supposed to own net-cash businesses that return capital, and Nvidia just authorized a record $150B increase to $235B of repurchase capacity on top of $120B of net income (+65%) and $215.9B of revenue (+65%) - it is now the largest capital-returner in the AI complex at the exact moment the hyperscalers halted theirs. Crucially it sits on the RIGHT side of the capex problem: the $602B the hyperscalers are spending in 2026, increasingly with borrowed money, lands in Nvidia's revenue line, so I get the AI exposure through the cash recipient rather than the cash burner. At 19.0x forward against 28.9x trailing it is the cheapest megacap I own on forward earnings, which is the opposite of the long-duration valuation risk a 5.2% ten-year punishes. The risk is that the capex it depends on is being debt-financed into a bond rout, so the 20% stop stays wide enough for its beta but hard enough to cap the loss at ~4% of NAV, and I take profits at +35%.

Held at roughly current size, up one point, because it is the clearest pricing-power compounder in the book: Q2 operating income +65% and net income +77% on revenue growth of ~53%, meaning margins are expanding faster than volumes - the signature of a monopoly raising price, not a cyclical catching a wave. It has an effective monopoly on leading-edge nodes, so every AI accelerator design from every competing customer funnels through the same fabs, which makes it a bet on AI compute demand in aggregate rather than on any one chip winning. Its capex is heavy at $60-64B but unlike Meta's it earns an obvious return, and it is being co-funded by customers and the $265B Arizona buildout. At 19.9x forward it is priced like a cyclical rather than the bottleneck it is. I keep it at 16% rather than larger purely because of the Taiwan-concentration tail risk that no amount of financial quality offsets, and the 20% stop and 30% take-profit reflect a name that gaps on geopolitics.

Cut from my 24% top weight to a normal position, not exited, because the business is excellent and the balance sheet trend is not. Alphabet went free-cash-flow negative in Q2 2026 for the first time in its history while long-term debt more than doubled to $98B against $175-185B of planned 2026 capex - by my mandate's own test it has stopped being a net-cash self-funding compounder, and the market is saying so, with the stock 16% below its $408 high despite a broad tech rally. The forward multiple of 25.5x against a 17.2x trailing multiple is the tell: consensus already expects the depreciation wave from this buildout to eat earnings. I keep a real position because the franchise quality is intact and genuinely improving - Cloud growing 82% y/y, Gemini expanding onto the desktop, TPUs giving it the only vertically integrated silicon stack among the hyperscalers, and a federal judge rejecting the DOJ's push to force divestiture of the ad exchange, which removes the single largest structural overhang. 18% stop.

New position, and the only one bought for what it does when my other four go wrong. CME is a genuine quality compounder on this book's own terms - a regulated near-monopoly exchange with open-interest network effects no competitor has ever dislodged, ~60% operating margins, minimal capital intensity and record H1 2026 revenue, adjusted operating income and EPS - so it belongs here on merit at 22.3x with a 4.3% yield. What makes it the right ADD now is that its revenue driver is the precise shock threatening the rest of the portfolio: the Fed has hiked to 3.75-4.00%, the ten-year is above 5.2% and the thirty-year is at 2004 highs, and interest-rate futures are over half of CME's volume, with August ADV of 29.7M contracts its second-highest ever and Treasury ADV +15% y/y. It is also paid twice by higher rates, earning interest on the enormous member margin deposits it holds. That gives me a rate-volatility hedge that is accretive rather than a cost, which is why I prefer it to simply raising cash to 4% in an inflationary regime. Sized at 11% and stopped at 12% because it is low-beta and a 12% fall would mean the volatility thesis had failed outright.

decisions.reason: My last leg was built on an explicitly wrong premise. I lifted gross from 70% to 88% on 2026-09-21 because 'the September FOMC event risk has passed.' It did not pass benignly: the Fed hiked 25bp to 3.75-4.00% in a 12-0 vote, its first increase since 2023, committed to an inflation fight driven by energy, and the median dot now points to one more hike this year. The 10-year has since printed 5.04%, its highest since 2007. That is a direct, sustained headwind to the exact factor my mandate is long - high-multiple small/mid-cap growth duration - and it is the opposite of the environment I sized up into. The honest response is to reverse the sizing decision rather than defend it, so gross goes back down to 70% and cash to 30%, which now earns a real 4% APY instead of being dead weight. Two legs are cut outright. NU is not a broken business - Q2 net income $1.1bn on 139m customers - but on 2026-09-26 Sky News reported it in talks to buy UK-based Monzo at roughly $11-13.5bn, and the stock lost about $6.6bn of market value on 2026-09-28, -10% in a session. That is an acquirer-dilution and integration overhang of unknown duration layered on top of an EM fintech already absorbing a US rate shock, and at $12.23 it sits only ~6% above my -18% stop; I would rather choose the exit than be handed it. XBI is the cleanest sell in the book: it is the purest duration asset I own, it is down ~8.3% over thirty days, and with the 10-year at 5% the catalyst density ahead does not compensate for a sector that has run straight into a rate wall. What survives is what is being carried by earnings rather than by the discount rate. I am not replacing the cut legs with new names - I looked at adding AI-optics exposure via LITE and rejected it because at roughly $880 a share it has become a ~$60bn large cap and sits outside this book's small/mid-cap mandate. Concentration into three positions I actually understand beats reaching for a fourth I diligenced in an afternoon, and the brief imposes no minimum position count. Churn is real: this trade replaces 35% of the book rather than all of it, keeping the three winners in place rather than round-tripping them through friction.
decisions.strategy: De-risked, concentrated small/mid-cap growth: gross cut from 88% to 70% into a live Fed hiking cycle, exiting the two legs whose theses broke (NU deal overhang, XBI duration) and concentrating the book in three earnings-backed compounders whose revenue growth, not the discount rate, is doing the work.

positions.thesis: Promoted to the largest position because it is the best growth-per-turn-of-multiple in the book at the moment multiples are the thing under attack. Credo grew revenue 157% year over year in its latest quarter - faster than Astera Labs' 104% - while trading near 40x forward earnings against ALAB's ~89x P/E and ~128x EV/EBITDA. In a hiking cycle the de-rating risk is proportional to the multiple, so within one theme I want the cheaper, faster leg carrying the larger weight. Its active electrical cables and SerDes/retimer content sit in hyperscaler AI racks where spend is contracted rather than discretionary, which is why this leg is one of only two in the book that is green on the current leg (+2.88% from 187.27). It is also the only name here with a lifetime standing-order fill against it, so I know it is volatile: the 25% stop is wide on purpose to survive AI-capex sentiment air pockets rather than being shaken out by one, and the 55% take-profit reflects that a 157% grower re-rates violently in both directions.

The single leg I own that is helped rather than hurt by the rate move, which is why it stays near full size after being marked down 5.55% from 123.30. Robinhood earns net interest on customer cash balances and margin books, so a Fed funds rate moving to 4.00% with another hike signalled expands the NII line directly - the stock sold off with a broad rate-sensitive fintech basket on a factor that does not actually apply to its P&L. Meanwhile the fundamentals accelerated into the drawdown: at HOOD Summit '26 on 2026-09-29 it announced 24/7 trading in native US equities including weekends, options hours extended 35%, intraday margin to 4x, in-app perpetual futures coming, and trading agents rolling out to roughly 29m customers. Volume is the monetisation engine and every one of those extends hours or leverage in which volume can occur. Through 24 September it had already done ~$267bn equity and ~$17bn crypto notional for the month, and BTIG lifted its target to $135 on 24 September against a $116.46 mark. Buying a widening fundamental gap at a lower price is the trade; the 20% stop is tighter than the semis because the drawdown here should be sentiment, and if it is not, I am wrong about the NII offset.

Kept, but deliberately sized below CRDO despite being the stronger franchise, because valuation is the transmission channel for a rate shock and this is the most expensive thing I own. Astera Labs is the rack-scale AI connectivity leader, grew revenue 104% year over year with Scorpio X ramping ahead of plan, and is the best-positioned pure play on PCIe/CXL fabric content per AI rack; it closed 2026-09-28 at 351.31, +3.10% on the leg, and is up 326% over the past year. Against that, it carries an ~89x P/E and ~128x EV/EBITDA, with sell-side flagging overbought technicals, continuing insider selling and rising stock comp. With the 10-year at 5.04% that multiple is the risk, not the business - a 100bp move in the long end is worth far more to this price than a beat is. So I hold the franchise and let CRDO carry the incremental theme exposure, trimming ALAB from 18% to a relatively smaller share of a smaller gross. The 24% stop respects that a name up 326% in a year has a long way to fall if AI capex sentiment turns.

Three things changed my mind since the 2026-09-16 leg. First, the hiking cycle is confirmed and extending: the Fed went to 3.75-4.00% on 09-16 in a 12-0 vote with 16 of 18 dots showing another hike, markets price ~65% for 10-28 and ~4.2% by December, with more into 2027. Against that, the engine pays a FIXED 4% APY on cash while SOFR-linked coupons reset upward at every hike. Cash is therefore a decaying asset in relative terms and floating-rate credit mechanically widens its advantage with each meeting. I cut cash 16%->10% and put the proceeds into AAA CLO. Second, FLOT no longer earns its place: it yields ~4.3% against a 4.0% risk-free engine cash rate, so I was accepting IG corporate credit and spread risk for roughly 30bps. That is the same logic this strategy already used to reject a Treasury floater, applied consistently - FLOT is sold in full and replaced by ICLO (Invesco AAA CLO Floating Rate Note ETF, 30-day SEC yield ~5.57%, 0.19% ER, $588mm AUM, $25.59 on 09-28), which pays ~125bps more for equal-or-better credit standing, since senior AAA CLO tranches sit above IG bank paper in the capital structure. Splitting the CLO core across Janus and Invesco also diversifies manager and deal-selection risk rather than concentrating it in one book. Third, I re-read why AMLP is down 3.29% while Brent trades ~$102: it is not trading as oil beta, it is trading as a yield instrument being repriced by rising short rates. At a 6.05% distribution it offers only ~50bps over a 5.57% AAA CLO floater while carrying full equity and commodity risk - poor compensation on carry grounds. So I size it as the hedge it is rather than as a carry engine: 20%->16%. I keep it, because the inflation the Fed is fighting IS energy, midstream posted record Q2 throughput, and it is the only leg that participates if oil keeps running. Net effect: blended carry rises from ~5.4% to ~5.8% annualized, the 66% floating block resets higher at every hike, and equity/commodity beta falls. Turnover is ~38% one-way at 2bps, roughly 2bps of NAV, which the added carry repays in under three weeks. I also widened the stops on the CLO legs from -5% to -8%. A AAA CLO fund's worst historical drawdown is ~2-3%, so a -5% stop is never hit by noise but could fire in exactly the liquidity air pocket where selling par-paying paper at the low is the worst possible action. This book's single lifetime standing-order fill was a stop that took it out of BTC-USD before a +30.68% rally; I will not repeat that error on instruments that redeem at par. -8% remains a genuine brake on a structured-credit catastrophe.

decisions.strategy: Beta-matched dispersion rebuilt for a Fed-hiking, 5.24% 10-year regime: a 55% long basket of eleven large caps across eleven sectors, screened for residual-to-SPY volatility and low pairwise residual correlation, with leverage-sensitive and secular-decline names removed and two rate-up beneficiaries (CME, TRV) added as the offsetting counterweight to the inflation-hedge legs (NEM, SLB), hedged with a 38% SPY short sized to the basket's 0.68 estimated beta for net index beta of roughly zero, 7% cash.

With the 10-year at 5.24%, the Fed hiking and 65%/53% odds of further hikes in October/December, hedging demand is structural - record ADV of 27M contracts (+23%), all-time open-interest highs in Ultra 10-Year and Ultra Bond futures, credit futures volume +164% YTD, on a 69.5% adjusted operating margin. Sized up from 5.1% because the thesis strengthened while the stock fell 3.4%, improving the entry. Its macro loading is the deliberate counterweight to the inflation-hedge legs NEM and SLB.

New. The most direct rate-up beneficiary I can own without taking credit risk: a $92.9B fixed-maturity portfolio with five-year duration, of which ~25% matures within three years and reinvests at the highest yields since 2007. Net investment income is already +14% to $1.07B with management guiding $840M/$870M after-tax fixed-income NII for Q3/Q4, and consensus EPS growth of +22.6%. Verified NYSE-listed at $363.16 on the 2026-09-28 close.

New. Managed care is one of the few large-cap pockets whose residual volatility comes from medical-cost trend and reimbursement policy - drivers with near-zero loading on rates, oil, gold or AI capex, which is exactly the orthogonality this book is screening for. Cigna raised guidance and grew profit in Q2 across both health services and pharmacy benefits, yet trades at $271.83 against a $357.76 consensus target. One of only three longs that worked last leg (+3.01% against a basket that was broadly red), which is evidence its residual is genuinely independent of the leverage factor that sank CHTR and CF. The -3.49% drawdown was sector drift, not a thesis break, and nothing in the research contradicts the original case. Trimmed slightly from 5.1% to cap combined healthcare-channel exposure alongside the new CI position, since both carry shared drug-pricing policy risk.

The second of three longs that worked last leg (+1.11%). Its macro loading is the deliberate inverse of LVS: persistently elevated inflation and a Fed hiking into a squeezed consumer pushes trade-down traffic into discount retail at the same time it pressures discretionary gaming spend, so the pair is self-offsetting inside the basket. At ~0.35 beta it is the lowest-beta long, materially reducing the SPY short the book must carry.

Best performer among the survivors (+4.32%) and the book's only technology exposure, deliberately chosen because edge delivery and security are subscription-driven and carry no AI-capex loading - critical when AI leadership is the dominant factor this book refuses to hedge into. Wider 18% stop because its residual volatility is the highest-quality dispersion in the basket and I do not want to be shaken out of the noise I am paid to hold.

The offset is that multi-decade submarine backlog is the most rate-insensitive revenue stream available, management guides positive FCF for Q3, Q4 and full-year 2026, and at $257 the stock is far below a $368 consensus. Smaller size is how I hold a genuinely uncorrelated asset whose near-term execution I do not fully trust.

Sized up from 3.7% and kept deliberately as the inflation-up counterweight to CME and TRV, which profit from hikes that succeed in suppressing inflation - if the Fed wins, the rate legs carry the book; if inflation stays sticky at 5.24% yields, gold does. Gold's pullback to $4,350 on hawkish signals is the entry, not the thesis break: at that price and $1,680 AISC on ~5.3Moz of attributable production the margin is extraordinary, and the stock at $116 sits below Bernstein's $157 and BofA's $151. Take-profit at 35% because gold equities spike rather than grind.

The single leg whose driver sits entirely outside the US rate story - Macau gross gaming revenue and the Chinese consumer - which is the highest-value orthogonality in the book when a common US-macro factor is what damaged the last leg. Macau Golden Week begins Oct 1, immediately after entry, giving a near-term idiosyncratic catalyst into peak seasonality; the stock has been upgraded on Macau share gains, trades at a 58% discount to its five-year average forward EV/EBITDA and at $39 against a ~$59 consensus. Oct 21 earnings sit beyond this week's horizon. Held at 4% because the China consumer risk is genuine and unhedgeable.

The oil-up leg, retained at reduced weight as the second half of the inflation-hedge pairing with NEM. Crude near $98 remains historically elevated and keeps international and offshore service pricing firm, and the -1.55% drawdown is immaterial noise rather than a thesis break. Kept as the smallest long because oilfield services is levered to E&P capex rather than the spot commodity itself, which makes it the less direct inflation expression of the two, and because SLB carries ~1.05 beta that the hedge must fund.

The beta hedge that makes this a dispersion book rather than a long basket. Sized by arithmetic, not by view: the rebuilt basket's weighted beta is ~0.68 on 55% gross long, contributing ~37.6 percentage points of SPY-equivalent exposure, so a 38% short leaves net index beta at roughly zero. It is smaller than last leg's 40.3% purely because removing the levered high-beta names (CHTR, CF) and adding TRV, CI and DG lowered the basket's beta. Deliberately carries NO stop-loss: the desk notes four short-leg stops fired last week on a 1.55% SPY rally, and a stop on an index hedge is self-defeating, because it removes the hedge exactly when a rally means the long basket most needs it and silently converts a market-neutral book into an unhedged long at the worst possible moment. Short borrow at 3% APR is the known cost of carrying it.

decisions.reason: Three things changed my mind. First, my de-risking went too far: 53% cash and four small legs produced +0.10% in ten weeks while SPY did +3.26%, because I owned almost nothing that could pay me. The fix is not more beta, it is more of the specific, researched event risk that is actually my mandate. Second, TEAM is a broken thesis, not a drawdown to be patient with. I bought it for post-earnings-drift with upward revision breadth; what has actually driven it is rate beta, with the 10-year touching 5%, rate-hike odds for the Oct 28 FOMC at roughly 65-85%, and software de-rating on negative margins and ServiceNow competition. It is -8.75% and 1.25% from its stop, so holding is just paying the desk to hit my stop for me. I cut it. Third, I researched the refiner trade that everyone is looking at and deliberately did not take it: ULSD cracks above $100/bbl are a record, but the proposed US diesel export ban already knocked VLO and MPC down 7% and 6% in a week, and that policy risk sits directly on the crack spread and cannot be hedged. I express the same oil event through XLE instead, upsized from 10% to 17%, because XLE is producer/integrated weighted rather than margin-exposed and it is down 2.11% over 30 days even as crude ran to $95-109 with global inventories drawing ~3.0 mb/d in 3Q26 - the equities are discounting a mean reversion the inventory data is not delivering. The genuinely new leg is BHF, and I want to be clear about why it is only 11%. I also checked the other wide spread on the screens, WBD, and rejected it: DOJ cleared it and the states settled on Sept 22, so at $30.87 against a $31.00 cash deal the spread is 0.42% and there is nothing left to earn. I also fixed a real error in my own prior book - my ACA take-profit was set at +3.0% off a 146.22 fill, which is $150.61, above the $150 deal price, so it was an order that could never fill. Removed. Net: gross exposure goes 47% to 62%, cash 53% to 38%, and every remaining leg has a dated catalyst rather than a view.
decisions.strategy: A three-catalyst event book: the CRH/Arcosa cash-merger spread as a non-correlated carry anchor, a sized stake in the broken-but-contested Brighthouse takeover where a rival bidder floors the downside, an upsized energy leg expressing the Hormuz supply disruption through producers rather than policy-exposed refiners, and a small index short against a Fed that has resumed hiking.

positions.thesis: Arcosa is being acquired by CRH for $150.00 per share in cash, an $8.5B enterprise value deal announced 2026-06-22. Stockholders approved it on 2026-09-04 with 39.6M votes for against 66k opposed - 80.8% of shares outstanding present - and there is no financing condition, as CRH is using cash plus committed debt. At the 2026-09-28 close of $146.53 the gross spread is 2.37% to a Q1 2027 close, roughly 6% annualized against 4% cash, which is a real premium in a year when merger-arb spreads have compressed hard (HFRI merger arb +8.2% through September, best nine months since 2021). I checked for a second request and found none reported; remaining conditions are HSR plus Australia, Mexico and possibly Investment Canada. The reason this is my largest leg is not the size of the spread but its independence: it is the only thing I own whose payoff does not depend on oil, the Fed or the index, in a market that has collapsed into one macro trade. Analyst consensus PT of $146.67 confirms the stock is now a pure convergence instrument. I carry no take-profit because the deal price caps it, and the 8% stop is a deal-break circuit breaker - a break returns ACA toward the ~$120 pre-announcement level, so the stop limits rather than eliminates that gap.

Brighthouse trades at $52.04 against Aquarian's $70.00 all-cash agreement that its own stockholders approved in February 2026 with 99.7% of votes cast in favour - a 34.5% spread on a shareholder-approved deal. The spread is wide for a specific, knowable reason rather than an unknown one: Aquarian missed the original closing deadline, and Delaware's insurance regulator has been questioning founder Rudy Sahay in closed session about his sources of capital, use of funds and plans for Brighthouse's balance sheet, with the equity running through an investment commitment from Mubadala Capital, majority-owned by the government of Abu Dhabi. That is a genuine risk of the deal dying. What makes it ownable at a size rather than avoidable is the underbidder: Talcott Financial, backed by Sixth Street, has written privately to the board reaffirming it wants the company if the Aquarian deal falls through, and Bloomberg reported on 2026-09-22 that Sixth Street is back in talks. So the bear case is not 'deal breaks and the stock craters to nothing', it is 'deal breaks and a second buyer takes the asset at a lower price' - and the stock is already at 4.1x earnings and a deep discount to book, 52-week low $44.51, only 14.5% below spot. I size this at 11%, not 20%, precisely because the resolution is binary and headline-driven and a Delaware denial would gap it; 11% behind an 18% stop puts about 2% of NAV at risk to buy a 34% payoff with a floor under it. Take-profit at 30% captures convergence just under the deal price rather than waiting for the last sliver.

This is the supply-disruption leg, upsized from 10% because the disruption stopped being a tail and became the realised state of the world. Strait of Hormuz interference has severed on the order of 14 mb/d of normal transit, Saudi Arabia shut its East-West pipeline, GCC-Iran talks were cancelled, and crude has run to the $95-109 range. The EIA's September STEO has global inventories falling ~3.0 mb/d on average in 3Q26 and a further ~1.7 mb/d in 4Q26, and says prices stay elevated until flows normalise and stocks rebuild. Against that, XLE is down 2.11% over the past 30 days and sits at $62.10 versus a 52-week high of $66.17 made on 2026-09-10 - energy equities are pricing a mean reversion in crude that the inventory draw is not delivering, which is the gap I am paid for. I chose XLE over the refiners deliberately: ULSD cracks above $100/bbl and Gulf Coast 3-2-1 at $39 look like the better trade until you price the proposed US diesel export ban, which already took VLO down ~7% and MPC ~6% in a week and which lands directly and unhedgeably on the crack spread. XLE's producer and integrated weighting is the cleaner expression of a crude supply shock and is not the target of that policy. The stop at 12% is sized for the real bear catalyst, a genuine US-Iran diplomatic breakthrough reopening the Strait, which would be fast and large.

A small, deliberately sized short against an index at $765.61 that is pricing none of the monetary tightening now underway. The Fed has resumed hiking for the first time since 2023 with a 25bp move passed 12-0, 16 of 19 FOMC participants' dots show at least one more hike this year, prediction markets put the 2026-10-28 meeting at roughly 65-85% for another 25bp, and the 10-year has briefly traded through 5% while an oil shock feeds straight back into the inflation print the Fed is responding to. This leg does two jobs: it is a directional view on multiple compression, and it is the hedge that lets me run BHF and an upsized XLE at all, since both carry equity beta I do not want unhedged into a hiking cycle. I keep it deliberately small at 8% because being short an index that has absorbed every bear argument this year is expensive - the desk saw four short legs stopped out on a single 1.55% SPY rally on last week's entry day, and 3% borrow runs against me. The 7% stop is set wide enough that ordinary squeeze rallies do not take me out, and I carry no take-profit because this is a hedge I want to still own if the tape actually breaks.

decisions.reason: Two things changed materially since the 21 Sep fill, and they point in opposite directions on the same axis. First, my DAL leg's thesis is dead. I owned Delta explicitly because jet fuel was rolling over; instead Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz was rejected by Washington on 28 Sep, Brent closed at $105.28 after touching $108.83 intraday, and BMO cut its Delta target to $100. The drawdown cause is not priced - it is live and worsening, which is precisely the condition my own mandate says to cut on. I am selling it despite it being a +1.85% winner, because holding it now would be an oil bet rather than a mean-reversion trade. Second, and symmetrically, that same rejection reverses the cause of my defense drawdown. LMT and GD did not de-rate on fundamentals; they fell ~3% on 22 Sep when Trump floated a negotiated end to the Iran war at the UN, deflating the munitions risk premium. That headline has now been repudiated by the President himself. Crucially, the defense case does not depend on the war continuing: the FY2027 request is $1.45 trillion, the largest increase since the Korean War, a $200bn supplemental is in train, and the Pentagon is pressing primes to ramp munitions already depleted by a war that has happened. Restocking demand is backward-looking and effectively earned. So I am adding to both. I also cut GS. Its decline is not idiosyncratic noise - it is the 10-year at 5.25%, the highest since 2007, plus BofA's warning on banks, and that cause intensified rather than resolved into the 28 Sep close. I looked hard at the 28 Sep 52-week-low list and deliberately rejected most of it: MCD is a value trap whose CEO told investors outright that conditions are not improving on the day it made a new low; LHX fell on a CEO ouster for conduct violations that is unresolved; OTIS has a CEO transition hanging over it until H1 2027; CHTR and CMCSA are secular decliners. Only XYL passes the test - a quality water compounder at $100.91, the literal floor of its $100.90-$154.27 range, marked down on financing for the $1.46bn Cornell/Roper pump deal whose $1.5bn of notes were priced on 15 Sep and are therefore done, against a Q2 beat and a $152 consensus target. I am raising cash from 22% to 25% rather than redeploying the full DAL and GS proceeds, because a 5.25% discount rate compresses every multiple in the book, breadth is poor (new lows have exceeded new highs for nine straight sessions, only 47.8% of the S&P is above its 200-day), and cash at 4% is positive carry against exactly the rate risk that is hurting my remaining legs.
decisions.strategy: Concentrated long book of oversold US large-cap quality whose specific drawdown cause is now priced or actively reversing - defense de-rated on a peace-deal headline that reversed on 28 Sep, an EDA leader that raised guidance into its selloff, a network incumbent marked down by target cuts while revenue accelerates, and a water-infrastructure compounder at the exact bottom of its 52-week range on an acquisition-financing overhang that is now fully priced - with the two legs whose drawdown cause is live and worsening cut and 25% cash held at 4% against a 10-year yield at 5.25%, its highest since 2007.

positions.thesis: The original thesis is being confirmed rather than merely hoped for, which is why this stays my largest leg. I bought Synopsys near 52-week lows on the argument that the selloff had outrun the business; since then Q3 FY26 delivered $2.477bn revenue and $3.91 non-GAAP EPS above the high end of its own guide, management raised full-year revenue to $9.715bn and EPS to $15.07 at the midpoint on AI-driven design demand, and HSBC upgraded to Buy on 25 Sep with a Street-high $700 target. At $417.61 that is roughly 28x raised FY26 EPS for an effective duopolist in chip-design software with the Ansys integration starting to contribute. I am holding rather than adding because this is the longest-duration asset in the book and a 5.25% 10-year is the one thing that can compress it regardless of execution - hence the wider 16% stop, which gives a high-beta EDA name room to shake out without stopping me out of a working thesis.

This is the cleanest cause-reversal in the book, so I am sizing it up from 15% to 16%. Lockheed fell 3.26% on 22 Sep to $517.95 for one identifiable reason - Iran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and Trump floated a negotiated settlement at the UN, deflating the munitions risk premium. On 28 Sep Washington rejected that proposal outright and Brent closed back above $105. The precise headline that caused the drawdown has been reversed by the same actor who created it. Underneath, nothing deteriorated: LMT is up ~38% in 2026 on real earnings, it just took a $1.2bn Army award for Precision Strike Missile Increment 2 after successful maritime flight tests, and the FY2027 request of $1.45tn is the largest defense increase since Korea. The important asymmetry is that a ceasefire would not undo the demand - inventories are already depleted and the Pentagon is actively pressing primes to ramp. I am buying a pullback in an uptrend, not catching a falling knife, so a 12% stop is appropriate.

Same reversal as LMT but a deeper discount and a different revenue mix, which is why I am adding a point rather than concentrating it all in Lockheed. GD is my worst leg at -5.58%, down ~10% in a month, and it fell to $343.82 on 22 Sep on the identical Hormuz-reopening headline now repudiated. The business did not participate in that de-rating: consensus looks for $4.14 EPS on $13.66bn revenue, up 6.7% and 5.8% year over year, and the company kept taking work through the selloff including Stryker and Navy combat-systems awards. Analysts have been raising targets by $5 to $68 on updated defense-budget assumptions. GD also diversifies the defense sleeve away from pure munitions toward Gulfstream and shipbuilding, so a negotiated Iran outcome hurts it less than it would hurt a pure missile prime. Keeping this smaller than LMT because the aerospace segment carries its own cycle risk with the 10-year at 5.25%.

A textbook sentiment-versus-fundamentals dislocation, so I am adding two points at a lower price than I paid. Cisco dropped 4.5% on 22 Sep to $106.44 on a Piper Sandler target trim to $125 from $132 - note the analyst stayed Neutral and his cut target still sits 17% above the current price. The bear case is memory component cost inflation compressing hardware margins and enterprise networking deceleration. Against that, the last quarter printed record revenue of $17.3bn growing 18% year over year with $1.22 non-GAAP EPS, both beats, and management guided FY2027 to $72.2-73.4bn, up 15% at the midpoint. Street consensus is Buy with a $133.86 average target against $106.74. A company accelerating to 18% growth does not normally trade at this multiple; the drawdown cause here is a revision of opinion, not of results. Memory costs are a real margin headwind, which is why this is an 11% position with a tight 11% stop rather than a core weight.

The single new name, funded by the DAL and GS exits, and the only one of the eleven S&P 500 stocks at 52-week lows on 28 Sep that passes my cause test. Xylem closed at $100.91, one cent off the absolute bottom of its $100.90-$154.27 range, down ~26% over a year. The cause is specific and datable: on 11 Aug it agreed to buy the Cornell Pump and Roper Pump businesses from Indicor for $1.46bn cash, then funded it with a $1.5bn revolver on 8 Sep and $1.5bn of senior notes priced on 15 Sep across 2029, 2032 and 2037 maturities. The stock fell 5.5% on the financing. That overhang is now complete - the paper is priced and placed, the rate is fixed, and what remains is an asset generating over $260m of 2026 revenue at 30%-plus EBITDA margins that management expects to be EPS-accretive in 2027. Meanwhile Q2 adjusted EPS of $1.46 beat the $1.34 estimate. Consensus is Moderate Buy with a ~$152 target, nine buys, seven holds, zero sells. Water infrastructure is also one of the few end markets genuinely insensitive to the Iran binary that dominates the rest of this book, which is why I want it here. Wider 14% stop because deal close is still pending Q4 regulatory approval.

My second-best leg at +2.44% and the quietest thesis in the book, held at roughly current size. Honeywell completed the spin of Honeywell Aerospace on 29 Jun 2026 at one HONA share per two HON shares, leaving the remaining company as a focused automation business across Building Automation, Process Automation and Technology, and Industrial Automation. Post-spin separations of this kind are routinely mispriced while index and mandate-constrained holders finish rotating out of the stub, and that forced selling is the drawdown cause I originally bought. It is now largely behind us and the stock has begun to mark up. The July acquisition of Johnson Matthey's Catalyst Technologies for $1.75bn net of cash adds process-technology content that fits the remaining portfolio. Process automation also gives real leverage to elevated energy capex with Brent above $105, which partially offsets the pain that same oil price inflicts elsewhere. Held at 10% rather than added to because the post-spin cost structure has not yet been proven across a full reporting cycle.

decisions.reason: One pair retired, one kept, one added; structure (two equal-weighted same-industry pairs, 60% gross / 40% cash) unchanged. RETIRED UAL/AAL. That pair was built on the 2026-09-16 divergence where UAL guided FY26 EPS $9-11 and said it recovers 80-90% of the fuel spike in Q3 and 100% by Q4, while AAL cut FY26 to -$0.65 to +$0.65 with ~$700M of unrecovered Q3 fuel. The fundamental divergence is still true, but its sign flipped: after Iran's diplomatic submission on the Strait of Hormuz around 2026-09-25 the geopolitical premium came out of crude, and softer jet fuel is worth far more to the hyper-fuel-levered, near-breakeven carrier (AAL) than to the one that already passes fuel through. That is exactly why the pair bled -2.52% on the long and only +0.37% on the short into the 09-28 mark. I am not flipping to long AAL / short UAL either: AAL already ran on 09-25 and 09-29, so that is day three of a squeeze, and it makes the leg a bet on whether Hormuz re-escalates rather than a company-specific relative-value bet. A pairs book should not own a geopolitical coin flip in either direction, so I take the pair off rather than pick a side. KEPT STLD/NUE at unchanged size and stops; the 2026-09-17 guidance divergence is intact but decaying, so it gets no upsize. ADDED M/KSS, where the 2026-09-10 prints give a cleaner and fresher divergence than anything left in steel: both retailers raised FY26, but for opposite reasons. Net effect is that I swap a macro-driven pair whose driver inverted for a pair whose driver is the quality of two guidance raises.
decisions.strategy: Two equal-weighted, same-industry relative-value pairs (STLD/NUE in steel, M/KSS in department stores), each built on a dated company-specific guidance divergence, run at 60% gross with 40% cash at 4%.

positions.thesis: Long half of the steel pair, held from the 09-21 leg at unchanged size. On 2026-09-17 Steel Dynamics guided Q3 to $5.34-$5.38 per diluted share with steel-operations profit significantly higher sequentially on metal-margin expansion across the platform and record shipments, driven by higher realized selling values combined with LOWER scrap costs. That combination - price up and input down at the same time - is the specific thing NUE did not claim. The leg is +0.17% since entry, so the spread has not moved against me and the divergence has not been arbitraged away. I am deliberately not upsizing: the guide is now two weeks old and largely priced, UBS upgraded STLD and NUE together on tariff support (which compresses rather than widens the pair), and late-September ferrous scrap export demand is firming domestic scrap into Q4, which is the one input that would retire the 'lower scrap costs' edge. 15% is the right size for a real but decaying edge, with the 15% stop kept from the prior leg.

Short half of the steel pair, hedging the STLD long dollar-for-dollar so the position is the spread, not a bet on steel prices. On the same mid-September guidance round Nucor guided Q3 to $5.55-$5.65, below consensus, and framed it as higher average selling prices and stable mill volumes being partly offset by rising costs, increased corporate expenses and weaker Raw Materials - i.e. the same revenue tailwind as STLD but with cost offsets STLD did not flag. The leg is -0.86% since entry, which is noise on a hedged spread. The one thing that would genuinely turn this leg against me is firming scrap, because Nucor's Raw Materials arm is a beneficiary of higher scrap while it is a pure cost to a converter; that risk is live into Q4 and is the main reason the pair stays at 15% instead of growing. Stop held at 15%.

New long half of a department-store pair, replacing the retired airline long. In its 2026-09-10 Q2 8-K Macy's beat on both comparable sales and adjusted EPS and raised all four FY26 lines: net sales to $21.675-21.825B from $21.5-21.75B, comps to +1.0-1.5% from +0.5-1.2%, adjusted EBITDA, and adjusted EPS to $2.15-$2.35 from $2.00-$2.20, with growth across all nameplates. That is an operating raise - the comp guide itself moved up and is positive - which is the specific quality the short leg lacks. This is the freshest dated company-specific divergence I could source, which is why it goes in at the same 15% as the steel pair rather than as a starter. The 18% stop is wider than the steel legs because M is a mid-teens-priced, higher-volatility equity where a 15% stop is inside normal noise.

Short half of the department-store pair, equal-weighted against the M long so the trade is the relative quality of two FY26 raises rather than a bet on the direction of US discretionary retail. Kohl's also raised FY26, to adjusted EPS $1.80-$2.40 - but the raise was driven by roughly $150M of one-time tariff refunds, and the underlying comparable-sales guide is still down 1.5% to flat. So the pair is long a retailer whose raise came from positive operating comps against short a retailer whose raise came from a non-recurring cash item while its comps remain negative; that gap should close when the refund stops flattering the compare. Sized at 15% rather than larger specifically because KSS carries heavy short interest and a 2025 history of violent squeezes, and the 18% stop is there to cap that: on a squeeze-prone short, being stopped out is the risk control, and I would rather take a defined 18% loss on the leg than hold an unbounded one. No take-profits anywhere in this book by design - each leg is half of a spread, and taking profit on one side would silently leave me unhedged on the other.

decisions.reason: Three things changed and all three are in the research, not in my memory. (1) The calendar event my book was built around has arrived: this book pre-committed 46% cash to an Oct-1 rotation into the midterm-year Q4 rally, and the entry date is 2026-09-30. Holding would be declining to execute my own mandate on the one date it specifies. The statistic still checks out: since 1950 October is the best month in midterm years, +3% average, positive 73.7% of the time, and the mean autumn-low-to-yearend move in midterm years is +13.6% vs +9.1% otherwise. (2) But the defensive half of my premise was falsified. My strategy of record said to wait for 'the midterm-year autumn low in early October.' There was no low. The S&P closed 2026-09-28 at 7,683 near record highs, 27 record closes YTD and ~13% up on the year; the statistically worst four weeks delivered a rally instead. I am therefore rotating, but NOT to full deployment: I take cash from 46% to 30% and gross from 54% to 70%, because buying a seasonal 'low' that never printed, into narrowing breadth (Morgan Stanley), a ~14% premium to fair value, a hiking Fed and a 5.25% 10-year, deserves a partial commitment, not the whole magazine. My mandate's own filter says keep only legs where the seasonal stat and the catalyst agree; for broad beta they now disagree, so SPY gets a statistic-sized 12%, not a conviction-sized one. (3) The energy leg was expressed in the wrong instrument. Oil is the dominant catalyst -- Brent ~$108, Strait of Hormuz traffic down 95% from 100+ ships/day to 5-12, Iranian officials signalling no deal before the November midterms -- yet my XLE leg is -2.44%.
