The Mag7 basket is up roughly 10% from the start of September while the average stock is down roughly 10% from its highs, a divergence the street is openly comparing to 1999-2000. With the 10y at 5.24% the discount rate on the longest-duration equities in the market is the highest in two decades. I keep this deliberately small because this exact short has been the widow-maker of the past year and because a 1.55% SPY rally stopped out four short legs across the desk on entry day last week; 4% with a 10% stop is a position sized to survive being early rather than one sized to be right.

decisions.reason: Three things changed since the 2026-09-21 fill. First, the higher-for-longer call stopped being a forecast: the Fed hiked 25bp on 09-16 to 3.75-4.00%, 16 of 18 dots carry another hike, core PCE was revised to 3.4%, and the 10Y touched 5.23% with the 30Y at 5.55% - the highest since 2007 and 2004 respectively. My TLT short is the only leg in the book the tape has paid (+3.89%) and it was my smallest long-side conviction at 8%. Underweighting the one thesis that is being confirmed is the error I am fixing: TLT short doubles to 16%. Second, my Japan leg is on the wrong side of its own currency. DXJ hedges the yen, and I owned it for a 'firming dollar' - but the BoJ is accelerating tightening, the yen has strengthened ~1.55% over the past month with USD/JPY back to 157, and hedged Japan gives that appreciation away. I am swapping DXJ for unhedged EWJ, which keeps the Takaichi-reform equity exposure and stops fighting the one G10 central bank whose currency has a hiking tailwind. Third, EWZ is my worst leg (-4.89%) and Brazil's general election lands in October, inside this holding period. The real's carry is genuinely attractive, but a binary political event is not something I am being paid to underwrite at 8% in an already-drawdown book, so it goes to zero. VWO is trimmed 16->10 because a firming dollar is a headwind to the whole EM complex and I would rather own the parts of ex-US that have a domestic rate cycle working for them than the broad beta. Gold's ~4% single-day break is not in this book but it is the tell that real yields, not growth, are now setting prices - which is the same signal that argues for short duration and for value over everything else. Cash goes to 16% at 4% APY, which in this regime is a real competitor to a marginal long, and gross drops to 84% because the book is -6.70% and I want the concentration in the confirmed leg, not in the size.
decisions.strategy: Broadening owned outside the US index-structure trade, now tilted hard at the one thing the tape is confirming: short long-duration Treasuries into a Fed that is hiking again, Japan switched from currency-hedged to unhedged so the BoJ tightening cycle pays us in yen, international developed value and European defense as the equity core, insurance geared to a 5.5% long end, emerging markets trimmed against a firming dollar, and Brazil removed ahead of a binary October election.

positions.thesis: The book's only winning leg and now its anchor. The Fed hiked in September for the first time since 2023, the median dot carries one more, and inflation is not projected back to target until 2029 - while the 30Y at 5.55% and 10Y at 5.23% show the long end repricing term premium rather than growth. TLT is the purest expression of that and it is a non-US-equity way to own the macro, which keeps me inside a mandate that is about avoiding the US index-structure trade, not about avoiding US instruments. Doubled from 8% to 16% because this is the thesis the tape confirmed. Sized at 16 rather than higher because two decades of yield highs is already a crowded short and the 3% borrow plus a violent risk-off reversal are the ways this loses; the 10% stop caps that.

Replaces DXJ as a direct correction of a broken assumption. I held hedged Japan for a firming dollar, but the BoJ is accelerating its tightening cycle and the yen has strengthened against the dollar over the past month - so the hedge is now a short of the one currency with a central-bank tailwind, and DXJ has gone nowhere (-0.23%) while EWJ's underlying market has run ~41% over the past year on the Takaichi reform agenda. Unhedged EWJ keeps the corporate-governance and reflation equity story and adds yen appreciation instead of paying it away. Japan is also the cleanest place in developed markets to own equities whose rate cycle is domestic rather than imported from the Fed.

International developed value, upsized from 9% to 14% and promoted to co-core of the equity sleeve. When real yields set prices, long-duration equity multiples compress and near-cash-flow value outperforms - EFV is heavy in European and Japanese banks and insurers whose net interest margins widen with the very long-end move that is hurting everything else I own. It has also been the most resilient long in the book (-1.15%). No take-profit: this is a regime holding I want to let run, not a trade.

European rearmament is a multi-year budget commitment funded by national defense floors, not a rate-sensitive growth story, which is why I want it in a book that is otherwise getting pushed around by the discount rate. Held flat at 12% - the -2.17% mark is beta, not a thesis break, and European defense primes are the rare ex-US industrial whose order books are insulated from both the dollar and the Fed. Wide 15% stop because the sector is volatile around headline risk.

Upsized from 8% to 12% because its thesis just got the confirmation the market gave TLT. Insurers reinvest float at the long end, and the long end went to 5.55% - the highest since 2004. The -3.26% mark is the sector trading down with equity beta while the actual economics improve, which is the setup I want to add to rather than cut. This is the one US-listed equity sleeve I keep, and it belongs: it is geared to the rate structure, not to the mega-cap index concentration my mandate exists to avoid.

Trimmed from 16% to 10%. The EM valuation gap to the US is still the widest in years and I do not want zero exposure to the broadening trade's biggest prize, but a Fed that is hiking again with the dollar firming is the classic EM headwind, and dollar strength hits the index through both currency translation and local funding costs. Ten percent keeps the option on EM without making the dollar the book's dominant risk factor.

Trimmed from 12% to 6% and demoted to a residual. With EWJ and EFV both upsized, VEA's broad developed-market exposure is now largely duplicated by holdings I own for specific reasons, and the part of it that is not duplicated is the growth-tilted half that a rising real-yield regime penalises. Kept at 6% purely as breadth so the ex-US sleeve is not three concentrated bets and nothing else.

decisions.reason: Three things changed and two of them indict my own book. (1) MU reports fiscal Q4 AFTER THE CLOSE on 2026-09-30 — my exact entry date. A 12% leg entering at that close is a blind binary on a stock that has already run to ~$1,054, with consensus EPS ~$31.5 on ~$51B revenue and a published estimate range of $28.04-$37.44. That is a coin flip, not momentum, so the standalone MU leg is gone; SMH still carries MU at ~5% of the fund, which is the exposure I actually want. (2) I checked the short book against the tape instead of my priors and found IWM is +17.2% over one year and up over 21% YTD. Shorting a strongly positive-momentum asset in a cross-sectional momentum book is a mandate violation that happened to be profitable for one week. It is replaced by ITB, iShares U.S. Home Construction, at -15.86% over one year — a real loser, killed by the same 5.24% 10-year that is driving my TLT short. (3) Measured one-year momentum says my mandate is right but my weights were not: SMH +87.0%, XLE +38.9%, XOP +33.9%, IWM +17.2%, ITA +2.0%, TLT -7.5%, ITB -15.9%. Semis remain the single strongest leadership by a wide margin so SMH goes up, and energy is the confirmed number-two leader with Brent at ~$105 and the Strait of Hormuz still shut, so XOP goes up. I checked defense (ITA) as a candidate and rejected it: the geopolitical headline is loud but the one-year return is 2%, which is not leadership. Net long is cut to ~34% and gross held near 84% because the 10-year is grinding toward the 5.40% and 5.53% technical targets and my longs carry a 1.73 beta.
decisions.strategy: Cross-sectional price momentum: long the two confirmed 2026 leadership complexes — AI-capex semiconductors and oil-shock energy E&P — against the two cleanest measured cross-sectional losers, long-duration Treasuries and rate-killed homebuilders, with the standalone memory leg removed ahead of a blind earnings print.

positions.thesis: The strongest cross-sectional momentum in the entire opportunity set at +87.0% over one year, and the only leg where the fundamental driver is supply rather than sentiment: top-five hyperscaler capex is tracking near $800B in 2026 and ~$1.3T in 2027, and Nvidia's own framing is a supply-constrained outlook with supply a bottleneck through fiscal 2028. Sized up from 26% because this is the mandate's core signal, but capped at 30% rather than pushed higher because the fund's beta is 1.73 and semis already took a >$1T drawdown in July 2026 — this complex can fall very fast when rates spike. Holding it via the ETF rather than single names also dilutes the 9/30 Micron print to ~5% of the leg instead of taking it head-on.

The custom-silicon/ASIC leg of the AI-capex trade, and the part of the complex with the longest contracted visibility as hyperscalers move inference onto in-house accelerators rather than merchant GPUs. It is my worst semi performer on the current leg at -3.61%, which in a momentum book is a reason to keep it at a supporting weight rather than add — held flat at 8% as diversification within confirmed leadership, not as a conviction add.

Wafer-fab-equipment exposure, the capex-intensity expression of the same cycle: Micron alone guided ~$27B of fiscal 2026 capital spending with fiscal 2027 running above fiscal Q4 levels, and memory capacity additions convert directly into WFE orders. Best performer on the current leg at +4.85%, so momentum confirms the position; nudged from 6% to 7% because it captures the memory capex cycle without owning the memory earnings print.

The number-two confirmed 2026 leadership complex at +33.9% over one year, and the leg whose catalyst is still live rather than priced: Brent closed ~$105.28 after trading as high as $108.83, Trump has rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and Iranian officials doubt any deal lands before the November midterms. Raised from 10% to 14% because I was underweight the sector that has actually led. E&P rather than integrated majors is the higher-beta expression of a supply shock, which is what a momentum book wants — and it keeps this book's symbols disjoint from the energy carry leg in my Round 3 book. The 14% stop respects that a Hormuz reopening headline would reprice this violently.

The cleanest measured cross-sectional loser at -7.51% over one year, and the position with the clearest forward driver. The 10-year closed at 5.234%, its highest since 2007, the 30-year at 5.56%, a 5-year auction cleared above 5% for the first time since 2007, and traders price ~65% odds of a hike next month and ~53% in December against a Fed that already went to 3.75-4.00% with 16 of 18 participants expecting another. Published technical targets sit at 5.40% then the 2001 high near 5.53%. Held at 15% and already +3.89% on the leg. I am paying roughly 4.95% of distribution plus 3% borrow to hold this, so it earns its size only while yields are trending — the 8% stop is the admission that a genuine growth scare reverses this fastest of anything I own.

Replaces the IWM short, which I found to be +17.2% over one year and therefore the wrong sign for a cross-sectional momentum book. ITB is a genuine loser at -15.86% over one year: home construction is the most directly rate-damaged industry in the market, and a 10-year at 5.24% pushes mortgage rates to levels that shut down affordability outright, with the Fed still guiding toward another hike rather than relief. Verified live at $88.75 on the 2026-09-28 close. Sized at 10% and stopped at 12% because heavily-shorted, rate-sensitive cyclicals squeeze hard on any dovish surprise, and this leg shares its macro driver with the TLT short — that concentration is deliberate but it is the reason neither short is larger.

decisions.reason: The regime call is confirmed; the expression of it was internally inconsistent. The 2026-09-16 FOMC delivered a 25bp hike to 3.75-4%, the first since 2023, on a 12-0 vote, with core PCE above 3% every month of 2026, a median dot showing one more hike this year and the market pricing further hikes into 2027. That vindicates the inflationary-hiking thesis this book is built on. But I paired that thesis with 22% in gold, gold miners and silver, and those are the assets that lose when a central bank hikes into inflation: gold is roughly 26% below its January record and down 6.5% in the past month on rising real yields and a firmer dollar, with sell-side forecasts calling for a further 5-20% correction. My own marks say the same — GLD -3.53%, GDX -5.29%, SLV -3.68%, the three worst legs in the book, and GDX and SLV are also the two highest-beta legs in a book whose mandate is explicitly net-low-beta. So I cut GDX and SLV to zero and halve GLD to a 6% tail hedge kept only against a Hormuz escalation, and redeploy into the parts of the mandate the regime actually pays. VTIP goes to 18% and I add 5% USFR: short-dated real carry plus a floating-rate note that resets upward with each hike, both near-zero duration, which is the correct anchor when the policy rate is climbing rather than the long-duration or zero-coupon real assets. Energy and commodities stay at size, not larger: the Strait of Hormuz closure has global inventories drawing 3.0 mb/d this quarter with total supply down 5.7 mb/d and Brent near $90, which is real cash-flow carry today, but OPEC and the IEA both cut 2026 demand growth and the 2027 Brent forecast is $74, so I take the carry with a stop and a take-profit rather than pressing it. The defensive-pharma sleeve is the one part of the book that has worked — AMGN +11.1% on the leg with positive Phase 3 dazodalibep data and a 6% dividend raise, GILD +3.07% on HIV growth and a raised outlook, MRK +2.61% and the sector's YTD leader at +44% — so it goes from 13% to 19% across three uncorrelated franchises, sized to respect the drug-pricing and tariff overhang. USMV and VLUE both rise slightly: min-vol is the mandate's low-beta ballast and value is the factor that a higher discount rate structurally favours. Net effect is the same strategy with the rate-sensitive leg removed and the rate-resilient legs funded by it. Zero symbol overlap with my Round 2 book, which is long semiconductors and energy E&P against short duration and small caps.
decisions.strategy: Net-low-beta real-asset and short-duration carry for a confirmed inflationary hiking regime: short-dated TIPS plus floating-rate Treasuries as the anchor, energy and broad-commodity cash-flow carry into a supply-constrained oil market, and value/min-vol/defensive-pharma risk premia — with the precious-metals sleeve cut to a residual geopolitical tail hedge because rising real yields, not inflation alone, now set the gold price.

positions.thesis: The anchor of the book, raised from 14%. Short-dated TIPS accrue CPI directly while carrying almost no duration, which is exactly the instrument you want when inflation is running above 3% on core PCE and the Fed is still hiking — the inflation accrual is collected without the mark-to-market loss that longer real duration takes as real yields rise. Its -0.39% mark since 2026-09-16 through a rate hike is the evidence: it did its job while the longer-duration real assets in this book fell 3-5%. Left unstopped deliberately; a stop on a sub-1-duration inflation-linked instrument would only fire on noise.

Energy cash-flow carry held at size rather than increased. With the Strait of Hormuz closed, global inventories drew 3.9 mb/d in Q2 and are drawing 3.0 mb/d this quarter, total 2026 supply is set to fall 5.7 mb/d, and Brent is holding near $90 — integrated and large-cap E&P free cash flow at that strip is the cleanest real-asset carry available and a genuine hedge against the energy-led leg of the inflation the Fed is hiking against. I am not adding, because OPEC and the IEA have both cut 2026 demand growth (OPEC to 580kb/d from 780kb/d) and the 2027 Brent forecast is $74 as Gulf production rebounds, so this is a carry trade with a horizon, not a secular long. Hence the 25% take-profit: if the supply shock pays out quickly I want to be taken out of it rather than round-trip into the 2027 supply recovery.

Broad-commodity exposure held at 11% as the diversified expression of the same real-asset carry, spreading the bet beyond crude into industrial metals and agriculture so the book is not a single-commodity wager on Hormuz. Its dynamic-roll construction is the specific reason to own this rather than a front-month tracker: in a market where inventories are drawing this hard, curves sit in backwardation and the roll is a positive contributor rather than the drag it is in contango. Stopped at 14% because a demand-led commodity selloff, which is the real risk if the hiking cycle bites growth, would hit every sleeve of this index at once.

Min-vol equity raised from 8% to 10%, funded by the precious-metals cut. This is the mandate's low-beta ballast and the reason the book's max drawdown is only -3.85% against a -8.61% drawdown in my other book. It is also the equity sleeve that behaves best in a hiking cycle: low-volatility names skew to stable-cash-flow, dividend-paying defensives whose valuations are already discounted at a high rate, so they de-rate less than long-duration growth as the policy rate climbs. Left unstopped as the intended ballast — stopping out the stabiliser in a drawdown is exactly backwards.

Value factor raised from 7% to 9%. A higher discount rate mechanically favours equities whose cash flows arrive sooner, which is the structural case for value over growth in a hiking regime, and it is the only equity-factor leg in the book that is actually up on this leg (+1.03%) while the real-asset sleeve fell. At 9% it stays a risk-premium allocation rather than a directional equity bet, which is what keeps the book net-low-beta. Unstopped for the same reason as USMV: this is a factor premium harvested over the cycle, not a momentum position.

Raised from 5% to 7% and the largest of the three pharma legs. Merck is the best-performing large-cap US drugmaker of 2026 at roughly +44% YTD, and the composition of that return is what earns the increase: it came from oncology and newer launches rather than from a GLP-1 obesity franchise, so it is not a crowded thematic trade riding the same flows as the rest of the sector. Defensive, dividend-paying and low-beta, which fits the mandate; +2.61% on the current leg. Stopped at 13% against the live drug-pricing and pharma-tariff overhang, which is a policy risk that can hit the whole sector's top line at once.

Raised from 4% to 6%, the best-performing leg in the book at +11.10% since 2026-09-16 and momentum backed by fundamentals rather than multiple expansion: positive late-stage Phase 3 data for dazodalibep in Sjogren's disease opens a new indication, and the 6% quarterly dividend raise is management signalling cash-flow confidence. At roughly +35% YTD it is the sector's second-best performer. Held at 6% rather than more because I am already running 19% total in pharma and the three names share one common policy risk. Stopped at 13%.

Raised from 4% to 6%. Gilead is the least correlated of the three pharma franchises — HIV rather than oncology or biologics — which is the point of holding three names instead of one. Strong HIV growth drove a raised 2026 sales outlook and a 3.8% dividend increase, and the leg is +3.07%. Recurring, price-inelastic treatment revenue is genuinely defensive cash flow in a slowing, high-rate economy, which is what this sleeve is for. Stopped at 13% alongside the other two.

Halved from 11% to 6% and explicitly redefined: this is no longer a core real-asset holding, it is a residual tail hedge. Gold is about 26% below its January record and fell 6.5% in the past month, and the cause is my own regime call — the Fed hiking to 3.75-4% with more to come lifts real yields and the dollar, the two things that set the gold price, and consensus now looks for a further 5-20% correction. Holding a large gold position while forecasting more hikes was the contradiction at the centre of this book. What justifies keeping any is the Strait of Hormuz closure: if that geopolitical situation escalates, gold is the asset that reprices violently upward while the rest of this book's equity and credit-sensitive sleeves fall together. 6% is the size at which that hedge pays enough to matter without the ongoing real-yield bleed dominating returns. The 20% take-profit is the hedge-monetisation trigger.

New position. Floating-rate Treasury notes reset their coupon upward with each hike, so this is the one fixed-income instrument that is actively long the path the dots are pointing at — a median FOMC member expecting another 25bp this year and the market pricing more into 2027. Effectively zero duration against Treasury credit, so it carries the rising policy rate with no mark-to-market exposure to it, complementing VTIP: VTIP collects realised inflation, USFR collects the policy response to it. Sized at 5% and funded from the silver leg. Chosen over simply raising cash because idle cash is fixed at 4% APY and does not capture the hikes. Unstopped — a stop on a floating-rate Treasury fund has no economic meaning.

decisions.reason: The memory-bottleneck thesis this book was built on has been confirmed by the tape and the industry data since the 2026-09-21 fill, so there is nothing to reassess and every reason not to pay for churn. Micron closed 2026-09-29 at $1,065 on a 7.17x forward multiple - the book was sized on the claim that bits were the single cheapest bottleneck in the AI buildout at 7-8x forward, and after a 120% YTD run the multiple has not re-rated at all, because earnings are running up as fast as the price. DRAM gross margin printed 84% and is guided to 86%, driven by price rather than volume, and advanced HBM4 capacity is sold out through 2026 under binding contracts. On the NAND side, SanDisk has signed long-term supply agreements with eight customers covering roughly half of expected fiscal-2027 bits, worth $93.9bn at floor pricing - that is exactly the contractual de-risking a commodity-bit book needs, and it is why I am willing to sit through TrendForce's call that NAND price growth moderates to low single digits in Q4 and turns down in H2 2027. The four legs are all within 4% of their fills (MU +0.96, SNDK -3.04, WDC +1.13, LRCX +4.14) and no stop is remotely threatened, so a replacement book would be the same four names at the same 2026-09-30 close, minus two round trips of commissions. The one real argument for acting is that Micron reports fiscal Q4 on 2026-09-30 with options pricing a ~10% move, and I am carrying it at 34%. I am deliberately not trimming into that. The fill is at the close, before the print, so trimming would be paying friction to reduce exposure to a distribution I believe is skewed my way: consensus is $31.73 against $3.03 a year ago, the margin guide is already in hand, and at 7x forward the valuation is not what a sell-the-news break normally requires. A 10% move on a 34% leg is 3.4% of NAV against 14% cash as ballast, which is the volatility this mandate is supposed to accept rather than hedge away. This book is down 7.09% from inception on earlier legs, not on this one; the fix for that is to let a correct thesis run, not to churn it on the eve of its confirmation.

The premise of the current book has broken and I am not going to pretend otherwise. This leg was explicitly 'a commodity-inflation book built around the live Saudi supply shock', two-thirds real-asset energy. That shock is unwinding in front of me: Saudi Arabia restarted the East-West Pipeline and resumed loadings at Yanbu, restoring roughly 3.5 mb/d, Brent fell 2.6% to $102.59 on 2026-09-29 and WTI fell 3.79% to $89.09, and the EIA now has Brent averaging ~$90 in H2 2026 and falling to ~$77 by 2Q27. When the supply disruption you were long resolves, the trade is over regardless of the price level. XLE and XOP were already my two worst legs (-2.44% and -5.70%) before that 2026-09-29 selloff, which is the tape telling me the same thing. So I am cutting XOP entirely and cutting XLE from 20% to a 10% stub, kept only because the US-Israeli war on Iran is still live and the Hormuz tail is discounted rather than closed. EWZ goes out: a Brazilian commodity-exporter leg is substantially an oil-and-iron-ore beta I no longer want, and at -3.39% it is not earning its 17%. GDX comes down from 15% to 12% - gold peaked at $5,608 in January and is down 6.5% over the past month to $4,151, so the policy-mistake hedge has stopped being a momentum position, but I keep it sized as a hedge. What I am rotating into is the one leg that actually worked, and its logic. COPX is my only green commodity leg (+1.27%) and copper just set records - $14,858/t on the LME on 2026-09-10 and $6.83/lb Comex on 2026-09-22, +48% over a year - on a genuine physical deficit: the Grasberg and Kamoa-Kakula disasters cut mine supply, H1 output fell, sulphuric acid is scarce and Chinese smelters are fighting for concentrate. That is a supply shock with no pipeline to restart, which is exactly what the Saudi one turned out to have. And copper's demand side is grid and datacenter electrification, which is where I add the rest: GEV, ETN and PWR are selling the physical layer of that buildout into backlogs that are already booked. This keeps the book in real assets and inside a picks-and-shovels mandate - I am still selling shovels, I have just swapped the barrel for the wire and the turbine. Symbol overlap with my Round 2 memory book is zero. I am holding 18% cash at 4% because the equipment names have run hard and drew a sharp de-rating scare on 2026-09-14.
decisions.strategy: A real-asset book rebuilt around the electrification bottleneck rather than the oil supply shock: copper miners as the largest leg, three grid-and-power equipment names selling into record backlogs, gold miners as the policy hedge, and a cut-down energy stub left only as a Hormuz tail.

positions.thesis: Promoted from a 12% tail to the largest leg because it is the only part of the old book whose supply shock is structural rather than logistical. Copper hit a record $14,858/t on the LME on 2026-09-10 (+19% YTD, +48% y/y) and a record $6.83/lb on Comex on 2026-09-22, driven by the Grasberg and Kamoa-Kakula mine disasters, falling H1 mine output, scarce sulphuric acid and Chinese smelters competing for limited concentrate. Unlike a closed pipeline, lost mine supply takes years to replace, and demand is the same grid and datacenter buildout that funds the rest of this book. I take the miners rather than the metal because at record prices the miners' margin expands faster than the commodity, and I take the ETF rather than a single name specifically to avoid Freeport, where the Grasberg outage that drove the price is also a volume hit to the producer. Sized at 22% - big enough to be the book's engine, not so big that a Goldman-style surplus call (their view is copper struggles to hold above $11,000) can break the NAV. Wide 18% stop because copper equities are high-beta around a tight physical market.

The purest picks-and-shovels claim on power generation for the AI buildout, and the one with the most contracted visibility. Backlog stands at $176bn and CEO Scott Strazik told Morgan Stanley on 2026-09-16 it reaches $200bn very early in 2027; Q2 2026 orders were $24.2bn at 88% organic growth led by Power and Electrification, with backlog up $13.0bn sequentially, and the gas turbine backlog is at 116 GW. Revenue this large and this far pre-sold is closer to a real asset than to a growth multiple, which is why it belongs in this book rather than a tech book. The risk is that the stock is up ~45% in 2026 and fell 9% on 2026-09-14 when GLJ started it at Sell with a $470 target, so the multiple is contested and can compress quickly - hence 14% rather than a headline weight and a wide 18% stop that gives the position room to survive a de-rating scare without being stopped out of the thesis.

The electrical equipment toll on every megawatt the datacenters install, and the most defensive way to own this theme. Eaton posted record Q2 2026 results with accelerating orders, total electrical backlog up 43% year over year, and total backlog of ~$22.8bn at 2026-03-31 with ~68% scheduled for delivery within twelve months - so this is near-term booked revenue, not a 2030 story. Management's framing that US datacenter backlog is 307 GW, roughly fifteen years of demand at 2025 build rates, is the same bottleneck claim I make about copper, one step downstream. I prefer it alongside GEV because it is a diversified industrial with aerospace and vehicle revenue underneath the datacenter growth, which limits the drawdown if AI capex decelerates - it also fell 7% in the 2026-09-14 group de-rating, so I am not paying the high of the move. Tighter 16% stop than GEV because a lower-beta name that falls 16% is telling me something real about the capex cycle.

The labour and construction bottleneck in electrification: the transmission lines, substations and interconnects have to be physically built, and the skilled crews to build them are scarcer than the equipment. Quanta reported a record $53bn backlog in Q2 2026 with raised guidance, which is the contracted-demand signature I want across this whole book. Held at a smaller 10% because it is the most execution-dependent leg here - a services business converts backlog into margin through labour cost and project risk rather than through pricing power, and Q2 commentary already flagged execution as the swing factor. The stock is also up 64% over the past year and fell 4% in the 2026-09-14 selloff, so I want the theme exposure without paying full size for the most operationally fragile version of it. 18% stop reflects that project-execution disappointments gap.

Retained, but cut from 15% to 12% and reclassified from a momentum leg to a pure hedge. Gold peaked at $5,608 in January 2026 and has fallen 6.5% over the past month to $4,151, which is why this leg is -5.29% and why I am not adding. What keeps it in the book is that it is the only position here that is not levered to industrial capex: if the AI buildout that underwrites COPX, GEV, ETN and PWR stalls, the likely policy response is easing into an inflation that has not gone away, and that is what gold miners are for. The operating case is intact even in the correction - Newmont posted record Q2 free cash flow of $2.2bn and Agnico $1.3bn, both inside full-year AISC guidance, so at $4,151 gold the miners are still printing cash rather than defending costs. 15% stop is the tightest in the book: a hedge that is losing this much while the rest works is a hedge that has stopped hedging.

Cut in half from 20% to 10% and kept deliberately as a tail hedge, not as a view. The reason I owned energy - the Saudi supply disruption - has substantially resolved: the East-West Pipeline restarted, Yanbu loadings resumed, flows are back to ~3.5 mb/d, and the EIA now sees Brent averaging ~$90 in H2 2026 and ~$77 by 2Q27. I am not paid to be long a shock that ended. But the US-Israeli war on Iran is still running and Hormuz risk has been discounted rather than closed, and a genuine closure would hurt every other leg in this book at once through input costs and a growth scare. A 10% integrated-oil stub is the cheapest insurance against that single correlated event, and integrateds rather than E&P because they carry dividends and refining margin and do not need $100 Brent to be solvent - which is exactly why I cut XOP outright instead. 30% take-profit is set low on purpose: if this leg is up 30% it means the tail hit, and I want to be taken out of it rather than ride a geopolitical spike back down.

decisions.reason: Two things changed since the 2026-09-21 fill and both point the same way. First, the drug-pricing overhang that has capped healthcare all year broke in my favour: Pfizer became the first major pharma to settle with the administration in late September on a most-favored-nation Medicaid framework, and with a template now public the sector-wide policy discount should compress. XLV is my only green equity leg and is still down roughly 3% year-to-date, so I am paying up for a catalyst that has already fired rather than for momentum. Second, the market found a new fault line: Meta's Muse AI agent triggered a de-rating of 'consumer inertia' businesses, hitting banks, insurers and brokers, alongside a 2s10s curve at its narrowest since March 2025. That is a direct problem for SCHD, whose financials and consumer-inertia weighting now carries a structural de-rating risk I did not underwrite when I bought it, on top of it being exactly the rate-sensitive dividend proxy my strategy of record already said to cut hard. So SCHD goes to zero and its weight, plus two points of cash, funds XLV from 32 to 38. Healthcare is the rare defensive sleeve that is cheap, AI-disruption-immune and now has its policy risk resolved rather than merely deferred. Energy, quality and min-vol are unchanged: crude at $89 with 5.7mb/d of Middle East production shut in through Q4 and global inventories still drawing is physical tightness, not a positioning story, and it is the defensive sleeve that actually works against commodity-led inflation. I am raising cash to 22% because the Fed hiked to 3.75-4% on 16 September with another hike in the December dots, the index has been consolidating for months, and idle cash is a paid, non-correlated asset at 4% rather than a concession.
decisions.strategy: Low-beta quality/defensive core concentrated in healthcare, where the drug-pricing policy overhang has just been resolved, plus high-free-cash-flow energy backed by physical crude tightness, with the quality and min-vol factor sleeves retained, the last rate-sensitive dividend-proxy sleeve closed, and 22% cash held at a 4% risk-free rate the Fed is still raising.

positions.thesis: The largest and only profitable leg of the prior book, sized up on a catalyst that has actually landed. Pfizer's late-September most-favored-nation settlement gives the whole sector a visible pricing template, which converts an open-ended policy discount into a quantifiable one and frees managements to deploy free cash flow into pipeline and M&A. XLV is still down about 3% year-to-date against a rising index, so I am buying a resolved risk at an unresolved-risk valuation. It is also the cleanest hedge against the two live threats to this book: it has no exposure to the AI-agent disruption theme repricing consumer-inertia businesses, and demand is inelastic to a Fed hiking into 3%-plus core PCE. Concentration here is deliberate - the brief imposes no size cap and this is the one defensive sleeve with a fundamental re-rating path rather than just low beta. A 12% stop, no take-profit, because the re-rating case is measured in quarters and I do not want to be called out of it early.

Held unchanged at 16% because the reason I own it is physical, not sentiment. Crude is near $89 with Middle East shut-ins averaging 5.7mb/d through Q4, OPEC spare capacity down to roughly 5.1mb/d, and the EIA projecting global inventories drawing a further 1.7mb/d in Q4 against a Brent average near $90. Integrated majors with high free-cash-flow yields are the defensive expression of that: they fund distributions out of current cash generation rather than out of a terminal-value story, which is what makes them work when the discount rate is rising. This is also the sleeve that pays when commodity-led inflation is what forces the Fed's hand, so it hedges the rest of a defensive book against its own worst scenario. The leg is down 0.58% and gave back more on the 29 September crude selloff; that is supply-headline volatility around an intact inventory deficit, not a broken thesis. Wider 15% stop to respect that volatility, 25% take-profit to bank a disruption-driven spike rather than round-trip it.

The quality factor sleeve, held flat at 14%. High return-on-equity, stable-earnings, low-leverage balance sheets are the right screen for a tape where the funding rate has gone up 25bp with more priced for December, because companies that do not need to refinance into a hiking cycle stop competing with their own interest expense. The leg is flat at -0.03% over eight sessions, which is the factor behaving as intended - it is not supposed to lead a rising index, it is supposed to lose less when the index breaks, and the desk's own note on increasing market fragility is the scenario it is underwritten for. I am keeping it rather than adding because quality is broad-market beta with a tilt, and the concentrated conviction in this book belongs in XLV instead. 12% stop.

Minimum-volatility ballast, held at 10% but on a shorter leash than the rest. It is down 1.20%, which is exactly what low-beta does while SPY grinds higher, and I will not sell a hedge for doing its job. The reason it does not get added to is that min-vol construction concentrates in the same utilities, staples and insurance names now exposed to the AI-agent de-rating that took Progressive and the brokers down this month - the very stability that earns a stock a min-vol weighting is what the disruption narrative is attacking. So it stays as realised-volatility dampener for the book, sized small enough that an insurer-led drawdown is an irritation rather than an event. Tightest stop in the book at 10%, because a min-vol sleeve that has fallen 10% has stopped being a min-vol sleeve and there is no reason to keep paying for it.

decisions.reason: The bank net-interest-margin leg is falsified and I am closing it rather than averaging down, the same discipline I applied to the short-semiconductor leg. I bought XLF on the premise that a hiking Fed widens net interest margin. The tape has now shown me the mechanism does not hold in this cycle: the spread between 2-year and 10-year Treasuries is at its narrowest since March 2025, so the Fed is lifting banks' funding costs at the front end while the long end - the asset side of the lending book - stays anchored. Hiking into a flattening curve compresses margin, it does not expand it. My premise was directionally right about rates and wrong about the shape that matters, and shape is the whole trade. A second, separate risk landed on top: Meta's Muse AI agent triggered a de-rating of businesses that monetise consumer inertia, driving XLF's worst six-day run versus QQQ since the SVB episode and taking the sector down 6.3% on the month, with Wells Fargo alone off 3.9% in a session. That is an unhedgeable narrative risk in a leg whose original rationale is already gone, and the fact that XLF now screens as cheap is not a reason to keep it - it is cheap because two independent things broke. The 12 points go to a carry engine with the same macro driver but an intact mechanism: senior floating-rate bank loans, whose coupons reset upward off short rates directly. That is the hiking Fed paying me a coupon instead of the hiking Fed maybe widening someone else's margin, and it carries neither curve-shape risk nor AI-disruption risk. I also add to the two engines the tape is validating - managed-futures trend, my only profitable leg at +1.72%, which is built to monetise exactly the sustained rate and commodity trends now in force, and commodity carry, where 5.7mb/d of shut-in Middle East production through Q4 and a further 1.7mb/d of inventory draw keep the curve in backwardation and the roll yield positive. XOP is trimmed two points to 9%: it is the highest-beta expression of the same crude view I already hold through AMLP, and crude fell 3.79% on 29 September, so I want the oil exposure weighted toward fee-based cash flow rather than drilling torque. Cash drops from 12% to 10% because the replacement leg is itself short-duration and cash-like.
decisions.strategy: Cross-asset carry and trend stacking with the falsified bank net-interest-margin leg closed and replaced by floating-rate loan carry, weight concentrated in the three engines a hiking Fed and supply-driven commodity inflation actually pay - broad commodity carry in backwardation, systematic managed-futures trend, and coupons that reset upward with the policy rate - alongside midstream and E&P energy carry and a covered-call premium sleeve, all long-only.

positions.thesis: The core commodity carry engine, raised one point to 23% and still the largest leg. This is a roll-yield trade, not a spot-price trade: with Middle East production shut-ins averaging 5.7mb/d through Q4, OPEC spare capacity down near 5.1mb/d and global inventories drawing a further 1.7mb/d in Q4 on EIA numbers, the physical deficit keeps the futures curve in backwardation, and an optimum-yield roll methodology harvests that positive carry every month regardless of whether spot goes up. It is the one asset that is long the same shock forcing the Fed's hand - core PCE has printed above 3% every month of 2026 and the hike cycle is supply-driven inflation, so this leg pays precisely when the rest of a long book is being discounted harder. The leg is down 0.36%, which is flat carry through a volatile month, and it takes no K-1. 12% stop, 25% take-profit to harvest a disruption-driven spike rather than round-trip it.

Managed-futures trend, raised from 20% to 22% and my highest-conviction add. It is the only leg in the prior book that made money, at +1.72%, and it made it in the month that broke two of my other theses - which is the entire point of owning trend. The current macro is unusually trend-friendly in the technical sense: a first rate hike since 2023 with more in the dots, a curve flattening toward its tightest since March 2025, crude held elevated by persistent physical disruption, and a dollar repricing off all three. Those are sustained, multi-month directional moves across rates, FX and commodities, and they are exactly what a replication strategy monetises long or short without me having to pick the side. Critically, it is the only sleeve here that can be short, which makes it the book's structural hedge against my own long-only carry bias - if the commodity or energy legs are wrong together, this is the position with a mechanism to profit from that. 12% stop.

New leg, funded directly by the closed XLF position, and deliberately the same macro bet executed through a mechanism that actually works. Senior secured floating-rate bank loans pay a coupon set as a spread over short-term rates, so it resets upward every time the Fed hikes - the 25bp move to 3.75-4% on 16 September flows straight into the coupon, and the additional hike in the December dots would too. That is a hiking Fed paying me directly, rather than a hiking Fed hopefully widening a bank's margin, which is the premise the flattening curve just falsified. Duration is near zero, so the curve shape that destroyed the XLF thesis is irrelevant here, and loans sit senior and secured in the capital structure rather than in the equity of businesses facing an AI-disruption narrative. The live risk is credit rather than rates - leveraged borrowers under higher-for-longer funding - but the Fed is hiking because demand and inflation are hot, not because growth is rolling over, and bank allowance-for-credit-loss coverage has been stable near 1.66%. Sized at 13% rather than the full 12-point rotation plus more, because credit spread risk is real and I want it as a carry sleeve, not a core holding. Tight 8% stop: a floating-rate loan fund down 8% is a credit event, not noise, and at that point the thesis is wrong and I want out mechanically.

Midstream energy carry, trimmed one point to 12% but retained as the quality expression of the energy view. Midstream partnerships earn fee-based, volume-linked tariffs with contractual inflation escalators, so revenue indexes to the same CPI that is forcing the Fed to hike while margin stays insulated from the crude price itself - this is carry, not a commodity-direction bet, which is why it belongs in this book alongside PDBC rather than duplicating it. The distribution yield is the return engine and it is funded from current distributable cash flow. The leg is down 2.61%, the worst in the prior book, dragged by the broad energy selloff into the 29 September crude drop of 3.79%; I am willing to hold that because volumes through the pipes are supported by exactly the inventory drawdown and production-replacement dynamic that the disruption is creating, and unit prices de-rated with spot crude that the cash flows are largely indifferent to. 12% stop.

Covered-call premium carry, held flat at 11%. The sleeve monetises implied volatility by writing upside against a low-volatility equity portfolio, and the setup for it is better now than when I entered: the index has been consolidating in a range for months with the desk flagging increasing fragility, which is the regime where a buy-write collects premium repeatedly without having its stock called away. Selling upside is the right trade-off in a market where the Fed is still hiking and the last two rallies have been given back. The leg is essentially flat at -0.25%, and the monthly distribution is the return I am underwriting rather than price appreciation. It stays at 11% rather than growing because it is still equity beta with a capped right tail, and this book's risk budget belongs in the commodity and trend engines that have a genuine asymmetry. 10% stop.

Exploration and production, trimmed from 10% to 9% - kept, but deliberately the smallest leg. It is the high-torque expression of the crude view: equal-weighted E&P names give roughly leveraged exposure to the oil price, so with Brent projected near $90 for 2H26 and the physical deficit intact it has the largest upside in the book if the Middle East shut-ins persist or deepen. But it is the same underlying risk I already hold through AMLP and PDBC, expressed in the form with the most beta and the least carry, and crude just fell 3.79% in a session on easing supply headlines. So I want the energy exposure weighted toward fee-based and roll-yield cash flow and only a modest tail in drilling economics. Widest stop in the book at 15% because E&P volatility would trigger anything tighter on noise, and a 30% take-profit to force a sale into a genuine supply-shock spike rather than let a disruption premium round-trip.

decisions.reason: The book is doing exactly what the mandate asks and the regime it was built for is still in force, so the only thing a rewrite would reliably buy me is frictions. NAV is +9.54% against SPY +2.24% with a -3.19% max drawdown, and this leg is nine days old (entered 2026-09-21). The re-tilt toward short-duration cash-flow value in a rate-HIKE regime is being confirmed, not refuted: the 10-year sits at 5.257%, the highest since 2007, the 2-year at 5.163%, core inflation is running 3.3-3.7% against a 2% target, and Governor Barr is still calling for more hikes. October hike odds did soften to 51% from 71% after Williams, but that is a change in pace, not in direction, and nothing in it argues for owning more duration. The mandated inflation-shock hedge is the leg carrying the book: XOM +2.67% and CVX +1.33% with Brent at $102-108 on a live Hormuz closure that Trump refused to negotiate away on 9/28. I deliberately keep that hedge in integrated majors rather than adding to it, because crude is whipsawing 3%+ a day on truce headlines and the majors' refining offsets damp that. The losers are ADBE -7.42% and ACN -6.25%, both long-duration multiple compression in a 5.26% world, but both sit far from their -18% and -15% stops and selling a capitulated quality name seven days and seven percent into a mean-reversion trade is the precise opposite of this strategy's edge. My one genuine complaint is PEP at 7%, a bond-proxy staple the strategy of record claims to have moved away from and which is structurally impaired at these yields; it is -0.84% and rewriting a nine-leg book to fix a 7% leg is negative expected value after 2bps a side plus SEC/TAF. Holding is the active choice here: the thesis is intact, the hedge is paying, and the drawdown is small.

I was wrong about where the trend was and the tape has told me so in a way I cannot argue with. This book is mandated to be quality-momentum/trend-following, and the last leg claimed energy, refining, commodities, metals and gold miners were 'the only relative strength the tape is actually confirming.' Seven of eight legs proved that false: XLE -2.44%, VLO -3.40%, XOP -5.70%, XLF -2.77%, GDX -5.29%, DBC -2.02%, XME -3.01%. Only the TLT short worked, +2.79%. The book returned -4.17% against SPY +3.26% while the momentum and quality factors it is named after led the tape. I was running a commodity-value basket under a momentum banner, and that mandate drift is the whole explanation for the underperformance. The decisive finding is a divergence I cannot explain away: Brent broke $100 and traded as high as ~$105 on renewed US-Iran fighting, with Hormuz crude flows collapsing below 2mbpd from 8-9mbpd, and energy EQUITIES fell anyway over the same stretch. When a sector will not rally on its own best possible fundamental news, the market is pricing the war premium as temporary, and a trend follower sells that divergence rather than buying the commodity story. My first instinct this week was to double down on energy because the catalyst was intensifying -- that is a fundamental value argument, not a trend argument, and cheap-versus-the-commodity belongs in my Round 2 book, which already holds the integrated majors. Second, gold is not behaving as an inflation hedge in this regime, it is a real-yield short: it has erased its 2026 gains and sits roughly 22-26% below its January peak, falling again in September to its lowest since mid-month, precisely because the 10-year is at 5.23%, the highest since 2007, with the Fed having hiked on 9/16 to 3.75-4% and signalling one more. That is a downtrend with an intact driver, so I reverse GDX from long to short rather than hold a falling knife. Third, my one substantive change to the rebuild: as first drafted it carried 30% short duration plus 46% long equity beta plus a short in gold, and every one of those legs loses together in a war-escalation flight-to-quality -- Treasuries bid, equities sold, gold squeezed. That is a genuine correlated tail, so I trimmed both the EDV and GDX shorts by a point each to fund a larger XLE leg, which is the only holding that pays in exactly that scenario. Net: I cut the entire commodity complex, concentrated into the one trend that is working, put the long side into the factors that are actually leading instead of guessing at individual leadership, and sized the hedge to the tail rather than to a view.
decisions.strategy: A trend book that finally owns the trends that exist: the confirmed US quality-momentum factor on the long side, the 19-year-high rates regime expressed short across the long end of the Treasury curve, a short in the gold-miner downtrend that rising real yields are driving, and one small retained energy leg as escalation insurance.

positions.thesis: The iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF is the most honest possible expression of this book's mandate and it has returned 25.29% over the past year while I sat in commodities and lost money. Sizing it as the largest leg is a deliberate admission that the index rebalancing into whatever is actually leading has beaten my own attempts to name the leaders. It also solves a real epistemic problem: I do not have high-confidence evidence on which individual names lead this tape, and MTUM rotates into them mechanically on 6- and 12-month price momentum without me having to guess. $20.8bn in assets, fully liquid, 2bps friction tier.

The only leg of the previous book that worked, +2.79%, and the macro has strengthened underneath it rather than weakened. The 10-year is at 5.257% and the 2-year at 5.163%, the highest since 2007, inflation is running 3.3-3.7% against a 2% target, Governor Barr is still calling for more hikes, and a closed Strait of Hormuz is feeding an oil-led inflation impulse straight into the long end. TLT is at 52-week lows, which is the definition of the downtrend this book is supposed to follow. I am roughly doubling it from 10% to 22% because concentrating into the one confirmed trend is what trend-following actually requires. Tight 8% stop because an 8% TLT rally would mean the rate regime genuinely broke and I want out fast; 3% borrow is a cheap carry for this.

The quality half of the 'quality-momentum' mandate, held as the factor rather than as stock picks, up 16.97% over the past year. High-quality balance sheets and stable margins are the right equity exposure specifically because rates are at 19-year highs: refinancing risk is what kills weak balance sheets in this regime, and QUAL screens it out sector-neutrally. Paired with MTUM it gives 46% confirmed-trend long equity beta that partly offsets my 30% short duration if inflation cools and both stocks and bonds rally together.

Vanguard Extended Duration Treasury ETF, confirmed trading at $56.15 and down another 1.00% on 9/29. Its effective duration is materially longer than TLT's, so it converts the same rising-rate thesis into more convexity per dollar of weight. Holding it alongside TLT is a deliberate doubling-down on the single trend I have the strongest evidence for, sized small enough at 8% that the concentration is a tilt rather than a bet-the-book.

A full reversal of last leg's long, which lost 5.29%. Gold works through real yields, not headline CPI, and with the 10-year at a 19-year high gold has fallen roughly 26% from its January record of $5,589 to $4,152, about 5% of that in September alone, despite a live shooting war that should have bid it. That is a downtrend with an intact driver, and the miners are the leveraged expression of it. Kept to 8% and given a 12% stop precisely because a Hormuz escalation or a dovish Fed pivot is the tail that would squeeze this, and I want to be stopped out rather than arguing with it.

Cut from a 39% oil-beta complex down to a single 6% stub, retained not on momentum grounds but as deliberate escalation insurance for a book that is now 46% long US equity beta. Trump rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait on 9/28 and over 20% of seaborne oil is still blocked; if that resolves violently upward, equities fall and this leg rises. I am explicitly not sizing it on the bullish crude story, because the whole point of this rebuild is that energy equities refused to confirm $105 Brent. 6% is the size of a hedge, not a view.
